P0A00.d: General circuit fault on temperature sensor A in the separate coolant loop that cools the inverter and other drive electronics of a hybrid or electric vehicle. The module flags it when the sensor signal cannot be used at all, without a more specific low, high or plausibility verdict; those cases have their own codes P0A01 to P0A04.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning light
Reduced electric drive power
Inverter coolant pump or radiator fan running constantly as a precaution
c: Corroded or loose connector at the sensor in the inverter coolant loop
Damaged signal or reference wire between sensor and hybrid control module
Fault in the input stage of the hybrid or inverter control module

P0A01.d: The sensor delivers a value inside its electrical range, but it does not fit the other temperatures in the vehicle. GM uses this code on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado and Sierra as a cold-start test: after the vehicle has stood for more than 28,800 s (8 h), the power electronics coolant temperature at power-up may differ from engine coolant temperature by no more than 30 °C, provided engi
s: Check engine light after two trips
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Electric drive power limited when the electronics are hot
c: Sensor characteristic drifted, reading offset against the other temperature sensors
Added resistance at a corroded connector shifting the reading
Low coolant or air pocket at the sensor in the electronics loop
Fault actually in the engine coolant or intake air sensor used for comparison

P0A02.d: The signal voltage of the coolant temperature sensor in the electronics loop sits below its valid window. Because the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage means an implausibly hot reading, typically a short to ground.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Displayed electronics temperature extremely high although the system is cool
Cooling fans and pump running at full output, drive power limited
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging signal to ground

P0A03.d: The sensor signal voltage is above its valid window, which for an NTC thermistor reads as an impossibly cold coolant temperature. Typical reasons are an open circuit in the sensor or its wiring, or a short to a voltage source.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Electronics temperature shown far below ambient
Reduced electric drive power as a safeguard
c: Connector unplugged, loose or with a pushed-back terminal
Broken signal or ground wire of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage supply

P0A04.d: The temperature signal from the drive electronics coolant loop jumps or drops out for short moments, then returns to normal. Coolant temperature changes slowly, so a sudden step that the physics cannot explain points to a loose contact rather than a real temperature change.
s: Warning light that appears and disappears
Short, unexplained drops in electric drive power
Stored code with no steady fault on re-test
c: Loose or fretting terminal at the sensor or module connector
Partly broken wire that opens under vibration or heat
Sensor with an internal intermittent contact

P0A05.d: The electric pump that circulates coolant through the inverter, converter and drive motor loop is driven by a control line from the hybrid module. P0A05 means that line shows an open circuit or a fault the driver cannot classify further.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric drive power reduced, especially in warm weather or under load
Follow-up inverter overtemperature codes such as P0A93
c: Pump connector loose or corroded, often from road splash at the low-mounted pump
Broken control wire between module and pump
Failed electronics or open winding inside the pump
Blown pump fuse or missing supply, so the control input sees no load

P0A06.d: The control line of pump A in the drive electronics coolant loop sits at a voltage below what the module expects for the commanded state, usually because the line or the pump input is shorted to ground. Depending on the driver design, the pump then runs uncontrolled or not at all.
s: Hybrid system or check engine light
Electronics temperature rising quickly, power limited
Pump silent when commanded on, or running continuously
c: Control wire chafed against the body and shorted to ground
Internal short at the pump's control input
Water or coolant in the pump connector

P0A07.d: The module measures a voltage on the pump A control line that is higher than the commanded state allows, typically because the line touches a supply wire or the pump input has failed internally. The pump in the inverter and motor cooling loop may then be stuck on or never receive a valid command.
s: Hybrid system or check engine light
Pump running all the time, even with the vehicle off
Possible power limitation if cooling cannot be confirmed
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition supply wire
Pump control electronics failed, pulling the input high
Output driver in the control module damaged

P0A08.d: General fault on the status line through which the DC/DC converter reports its condition to the hybrid control module. The converter replaces the alternator: it steps the traction battery voltage down to charge the 12 V battery.
s: Hybrid system, battery or master warning light on
12 V battery is no longer charged and voltage drops while driving
Electrical consumers fail and the hybrid system may finally shut down
c: Internal fault in the DC/DC converter reported by its self-diagnosis
Damaged or corroded status line or connector between converter and hybrid control module
Converter overheating due to a fault in the inverter/converter coolant loop
Faulty input stage in the hybrid control module

P0A09.d: The status signal that the DC/DC converter sends to the hybrid control module stays below its expected range, typically from a short to ground, an open line read as low, or a converter that pulls its status output down because of an internal fault. Mitsubishi uses P0A09 on the 2012-2013 i-MiEV for a DC-DC converter fault; its bulletins tie it to a failed on-board charger that blows the high-voltage fuse feeding the c
s: Power unit, battery or hybrid warning light on
12 V battery not charged, voltage drops
On EVs the drive battery may also stop charging
c: Blown high-voltage fuse feeding the converter, e.g. after an on-board charger failure (Mitsubishi i-MiEV)
DC/DC converter internal fault pulling the status output low
Status line shorted to ground or chafed harness
Faulty input stage in the hybrid/EV control module

P0A0A.d: The high-voltage interlock loop (HVIL) is a low-voltage signal loop routed through every HV connector, the service disconnect and component covers. If it opens, the control module opens the main contactors so no one can touch live parts.
s: Vehicle will not start or go into ready mode
Check engine and hybrid system warning on
High-voltage system switched off while the 12 V system still works
c: HV connector or service disconnect not fully seated after repair
Spread, bent or corroded interlock pins or damaged connector seals
Battery pack control module software fault (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid 2024-2025)

P0A0B.d: The interlock loop A responds electrically, but its behaviour does not match what the module expects – for example a loop resistance outside the window, a signal that does not follow the commanded test pattern, or two modules on the same loop disagreeing. Mercedes-Benz logs P0A0B00 in the battery management system, the DC converter and the on-board charger of model line 243 when the vehicle will not start; its listed
s: Vehicle cannot be started
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
Several modules store interlock codes at the same time
c: Oxidised interlock pins in low-voltage connectors raising loop resistance
Improperly connected HV connector or bent interlock pins on an HV component
Twisted or chafed interlock harness rubbing on the body
Faulty interlock driver or receiver in a control module

P0A0C.d: The voltage sensed on interlock loop A is too low while the module drives the loop – typically an opened loop or a short to ground. GM documents it codegenau: in its 2016 HPC2 table P0A0C sets when the sensed interlock voltage stays below 30 % of the 5 V test signal in 2 of 2 samples (12.5 ms each) with the 12 V supply above 10.2 V; it is Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip.
s: Check engine light (GM Type A) and hybrid/EV warning
No ready mode, electric drive unavailable
Charging may be blocked
c: HV connector, cover or service disconnect open, interrupting the loop
Interlock wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed at a module or the body
Faulty interlock source or sense stage in the battery or hybrid module

P0A0D.d: The voltage sensed on interlock loop A is higher than expected – most often a short to a voltage source, or the loop not being pulled down when the module expects it. GM checks both states: in the 2016 HPC2 table P0A0D sets when the sensed voltage exceeds 24 % of 5 V with the source switched off (5 of 8 samples) or 44 % with it switched on (4 of 6 samples), Type A with MIL after one trip.
s: No ready mode or ready light blinking
Check engine and charging warning lights on
Vehicle cannot be started
c: Service/safety plug not fully inserted or with poor contact (Hyundai Sonata Hybrid)
Interlock wire shorted to a 12 V or reference voltage
Damaged interlock harness or connector after body or battery work
Faulty interlock stage in the battery or hybrid control module

P0A0E.d: The interlock loop A signal drops out or jumps for short moments and then recovers, so the module sees an unstable loop rather than a lasting open or short. Typical are connectors with loose or spread contacts, harness sections that move with the body or drivetrain, and moisture in seals.
s: Hybrid/EV warning that appears and disappears
Occasional loss of ready mode or sudden shutdown of electric drive
Intermittent no-start, often after rough roads or rain
c: Loose or spread interlock contacts in an HV or low-voltage connector
Harness section with a broken strand that opens under vibration
Moisture entering through a damaged connector seal
Electrical interference on the interlock line or a weak module input

P0A0F.d: The control module commanded an engine start – by the hybrid system or an automatic start/stop restart – but the combustion engine did not reach a self-sustaining run within the allowed attempts. The code describes the result, not the cause.
s: Check engine light and hybrid or drive system warning
Engine does not start, or runs briefly and stops
Reduced power because the vehicle runs on the battery only
c: Vacuum leak, e.g. separated purge VSV/PCV hose at the throttle body (Toyota Prius)
Shorted sensor harness pulling down the engine ECU 5 V reference (Kia Niro)
Fuel delivery or ignition fault preventing combustion
Failed automatic restart of a mild hybrid with a cold engine (Audi A6/A7 2019)

P0A10.d: The status signal from the DC/DC converter to the hybrid control module sits above its valid range, typically because the line is shorted to a voltage source, its ground or pull-down path is open, or the converter drives the output high after an internal failure. The converter supplies the 12 V system from the traction battery, and its self-diagnosis reports problems over this status path.
s: Hybrid system or battery warning light on
12 V battery voltage falls while driving
Possible shutdown of the hybrid system if the 12 V battery runs flat
c: Status line shorted to 12 V or another supply
Open ground or signal return at the converter connector
DC/DC converter internal fault driving the status output high
Faulty input stage in the hybrid control module

P0A11.d: General or open-circuit fault on the enable line with which the hybrid or battery control module tells the DC/DC converter that it may deliver power to the 12 V system. In typical designs a high enable level permits converter output, and a CAN message carries the same permission in parallel, so the two can be cross-checked.
s: Battery or charging warning light on
12 V battery is not charged and runs down
Vehicle may lose motive power after a while
c: Broken enable wire or unplugged connector between control module and converter
Corroded or pushed-out terminal at the converter enable pin
Faulty enable output driver in the control module
Faulty enable input inside the DC/DC converter

P0A12.d: The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads low when the control module is commanding it on. Because a low enable level usually means converter output is not permitted, the converter stays off and the 12 V system loses its charging source.
s: Charging or battery warning light on
12 V voltage drops, electrical consumers misbehave
Hybrid system may shut down when the 12 V battery is flat
c: Weak or failed enable output driver in the control module

P0A13.d: The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads high when the control module expects it low, for example while the converter should be switched off. The usual reasons are a short to battery voltage on the enable wire, a stuck output driver, or a missing pull-down.
s: Hybrid system or battery warning light on
12 V battery drains while the vehicle is parked
Converter-related functions disabled as a precaution
c: Enable wire shorted to 12 V or another supply
Enable output driver in the control module stuck on
Open pull-down or ground reference at the converter input

P0A14.d: Some vehicles use switchable or active engine mounts that the powertrain or a mount control unit changes between soft and firm, or drives with an actuator against vibration. P0A14 reports an open or undefined fault in the control circuit of mount A.
s: More vibration at idle or during cylinder deactivation
Warning light, depending on manufacturer
Shudder that feels like a torque converter problem
c: Mount actuator connector loose, corroded or unplugged after engine work
Open coil in the mount actuator or switching solenoid
Wire broken where the harness flexes with engine movement
Fault in the engine or mount control unit output

P0A15.d: The control circuit of switchable or active engine mount A shows a voltage or current below the expected level, which usually points to a short to ground on the line or inside the actuator. Ford uses P0A15 in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary for the active mounts: the low-level driver reports the fault and the PCM matures it after about 5 seconds; the partner mount B has P0AB7.
s: Noticeable vibration at idle or low speed
Warning light, depending on manufacturer
Cylinder deactivation may be suppressed
c: Control wire chafed on the engine or subframe and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the mount actuator or solenoid, often after fluid leakage

P0A16.d: The module sees a higher voltage on the control circuit of engine mount A than it should for the commanded state, usually a short to a supply line or a failed actuator input. The mount can then no longer be switched or driven as intended.
s: Harsh idle or more engine movement on take-off
Warning light, depending on manufacturer
Vibration during cylinder deactivation
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition supply
Mount actuator or solenoid failed with an open low side
Driver stage in the engine or mount control unit damaged

P0A17.d: Some electric drive units measure the torque on the motor or generator shaft directly, for example with a magnetostrictive sensor inside a hollow motor shaft as described in Honda patents for hybrid drive systems. The control unit uses that value to check the torque it commands.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Electric drive power limited or electric drive disabled
Higher fuel consumption because the engine runs more often
c: Loose or corroded sensor connector at the drive unit
Damaged sensor wiring between drive unit and control module
Torque sensor or its excitation electronics failed, often only replaceable with the drive unit
Input stage of the hybrid or motor control module faulty

P0A18.d: The motor torque sensor delivers an electrically valid signal, but the torque it reports does not match what the control unit expects from the commanded motor current, speed and operating state. Typical checks compare measured and estimated torque or look for an offset when no torque is applied.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Reduced or uneven electric assistance
Engine runs more often, fuel use rises
c: Sensor offset or gain drifted, reading off against the torque model
Electrical interference on the signal from damaged shielding or ground
Missing or outdated calibration after module or drive unit replacement
Mechanical fault in the drive unit that changes the real torque

P0A19.d: The control unit watches the voltage of a torque sensor that measures load directly on the traction motor shaft, such as the magnetostrictive sensor in a hollow motor shaft shown in a Honda patent. P0A19 sets when the signal stays below its valid window for a calibrated time, typical of a short to ground, a broken supply or an open signal line pulled low.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Reduced electric drive power or electric drive disabled
Engine runs more often, higher fuel consumption
c: Sensor signal or supply line shorted to ground
Sensor reference or excitation supply missing
Corroded or loose connector at the drive unit
Torque sensor electronics failed, often replaced with the drive unit

P0A1A.d: P0A1A reports a fault of the electronics that control the generator, either inside a hybrid inverter or in a belt starter-generator. Toyota lists P0A1A for the 2010-2015 Prius and 2012-2017 Prius V together with P0A94, P324E and P3004 as a malfunction inside the inverter assembly with converter; the repair can mean replacing the MG ECU, IPM transistors or the whole inverter.
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Battery no longer charged, start-stop or hybrid drive unavailable
Vehicle may not reach ready state
c: Internal failure of the inverter or generator control electronics
Control software fault, fixed by an update where the maker provides one
Supply, ground or bus connection to the module faulty

P0A1B.d: P0A1B flags a self-test failure of the processor that controls drive motor A, usually inside the inverter. In GM hybrid tables (2016) it sets when the processor fails an inhibit path test at power-down, three or more times, proving it could not take the system to a safe state; in 2011 tables internal SPI, RAM or cache faults in 28 of 32 samples count.
s: Loss of drive warning and MIL
Vehicle cannot be driven electrically or not at all
Fault may vanish after a full sleep cycle while the code stays stored
c: Control software fault, several makers resolve it by reprogramming
Internal processor or memory fault in the inverter control board
Weak 12 V supply during start-up or shutdown

P0A1C.d: P0A1C is the counterpart of P0A1B for the second electric machine, drive motor B, and reports that its control processor is no longer trustworthy. GM hybrid tables use it for the motor control processor B: in 2016 calibrations the code sets when an inhibit path test at power-down fails three or more times, in 2011 calibrations internal processor integrity faults such as SPI, RAM or cache errors are counted.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Reduced drive power or no electric drive
c: Internal processor or memory fault on the motor B control board
Calibration or software fault in the inverter
Unstable 12 V supply or ground to the inverter electronics

P0A1D.d: The hybrid powertrain control module coordinates engine, motors and battery. P0A1D says this module has reported an internal failure or is no longer working reliably.
s: MIL and hybrid warning on
Engine power reduced
Hybrid functions limited or unavailable
c: Internal fault of the hybrid control module
Code stored by a scan tool communication error, not by a real defect
Supply, ground or network fault at the module

P0A1E.d: Mild and full hybrids often start the engine and recharge the battery with a belt-driven starter-generator that has its own control electronics. P0A1E means that controller has reported a fault or works incorrectly.
s: Wrench lamp or MIL on, electrical system warning
Auto start-stop disabled
Electric-only driving unavailable
c: Loose wiring connection at the starter-generator
Starter-generator software fault, fixed by update

P0A1F.d: The battery energy control module supervises cell voltages, current and temperatures of the high-voltage pack. P0A1F reports that this module failed its own integrity checks.
s: MIL or service engine soon light on
Battery or hybrid warning, limited electric operation
Start-stop may be disabled
c: Module software fault, fixed by a new calibration
Internal hardware fault of the battery control module
Unstable 12 V supply causing module resets

P0A20.d: This code covers the upper electrical limit of a torque sensor fitted to the traction motor shaft, for example the magnetostrictive design inside a hollow output shaft described in a Honda patent. The control unit sets P0A20 when the sensor voltage remains above the valid range for a calibrated time, which points to a short to the supply voltage, an open ground return or a sensor output stuck high.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Electric drive torque limited
Reduced acceleration in electric mode
c: Signal line shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage

P0A21.d: Here the torque sensor on the traction motor shaft delivers a signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing permanently. Such shaft sensors, as in the Honda patent with a sensor inside a hollow motor shaft, sit in an area with strong electromagnetic fields and vibration, so loose terminals, chafed wires and interference are the usual suspects.
s: Hybrid warning that appears and disappears
Brief loss of electric assist
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed sensor wiring that shorts briefly under vibration
Damaged shield letting inverter noise into the signal

P0A22.d: In series or power-split hybrids a separate electric machine runs as generator, driven by the combustion engine. A Honda patent claims a torque sensor inside the hollow shaft of either the traction motor or this generator.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Reduced battery charging by the engine
Limited system power
c: Sensor connector at the generator unplugged, loose or corroded
Open circuit in the sensor harness
Generator torque sensor or its electronics failed

P0A23.d: The generator torque sensor sends an electrically valid voltage, but the torque it reports does not fit the generator current, speed and engine load the control unit knows. Typical checks compare the measured value with a torque model or look for an offset while the generator is idle.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Generator output limited, battery charges slowly
c: Sensor zero point or gain drifted
Electromagnetic interference from the generator or inverter
Contact resistance in the connector skewing the signal

P0A24.d: P0A24 is stored when the voltage from the generator torque sensor stays under its lower diagnostic limit for a calibrated time. Electrically this means the line is pulled toward ground, the sensor supply is missing or the signal wire is broken.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Reduced charging and system power
c: Sensor electronics failed with output stuck low

P0A25.d: With P0A25 the control unit sees the generator torque sensor signal above its permitted upper limit for longer than the calibrated debounce time. The common electrical explanations are a short from the signal line to the supply or battery voltage, an interrupted sensor ground, or a sensor output stuck at its maximum.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Generator output limited
c: Signal line shorted to supply or battery voltage

P0A26.d: P0A26 points to short interruptions or jumps in the generator torque sensor signal rather than a constant fault. The control unit counts implausible signal changes or brief out-of-range events and sets the code once a calibrated limit is exceeded.
s: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Brief drop in charging or system power
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed wiring near the generator housing
Shield or ground damage letting inverter noise in

P0A27.d: P0A27 covers the circuit that tells the high-voltage battery to drop off the bus, i.e. the command path that opens the main contactors at key-off, after a fault or after a crash signal.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Vehicle will not enter ready mode or shuts down while driving
High-voltage system does not power down after key-off
c: Contactor or its driver does not release when power-off is commanded
Internal fault in the inverter/power unit that controls the contactors (Honda Civic Hybrid)
Damaged wiring or loose terminal on the hardwired power-off line
Crash or emergency shutdown signal stored or still active

P0A28.d: The control unit watches the voltage on the line that commands the high-voltage battery to disconnect. P0A28 sets when that signal stays below its valid window for a calibrated time, typical of a short to ground or a lost supply on the line.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Vehicle does not reach ready mode
Electric drive disabled, engine runs constantly
c: Power-off signal line shorted to ground
Poor terminal fit or corrosion at the battery or control module connector
Missing supply or blown fuse feeding the power-off circuit
Faulty driver stage in the battery or hybrid control module

P0A29.d: P0A29 is stored when the voltage on the hybrid battery power-off line sits above its plausible range for longer than allowed, which points to an open line pulled up internally or a short to a supply voltage. No manufacturer explains P0A29 publicly; GM merely names it as a keyword in a generic bulletin on terminal fit.
s: Hybrid system warning light
Vehicle does not reach ready mode
High-voltage system stays active after switching off
c: Open power-off line or unplugged connector
Power-off line shorted to battery voltage
Spread or corroded terminals at the connectors
Faulty input or driver stage in the control module

P0A2A.d: A thermistor in the stator of traction motor A reports winding temperature so the inverter can cut torque before the insulation overheats. P0A2A is the general circuit fault; the failure type sits in the extension byte.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Reduced electric drive power
Implausible motor temperature in live data
c: Broken or shorted sensor wire between motor and inverter
Loose or corroded connector at the drive unit
Thermistor failed inside the motor or transaxle
Faulty sensor input in the inverter/motor control module

P0A2B.d: This is the rationality check: after a long soak, motor A's temperature should match other temperatures in the drive. GM compares it with the average inverter module temperature on its 2013 two-mode trucks and sets P0A2B, Type B, if they differ by more than 28 °C after at least 360 minutes off; the 2011 table uses 20 °C against coolant and transmission fluid, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid 25 °C.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric drive power limited
Motor temperature far off from other temperatures after a cold soak
c: Thermistor drifted out of its resistance curve
Added resistance from a worn or corroded connector (Audi A7 e quattro)
Fault in a reference temperature such as inverter or fluid temperature
Motor cooling problem that makes a real temperature look implausible

P0A2C.d: The motor A sensor is an NTC thermistor, so its signal voltage falls as the winding heats; Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid bulletin gives about 11 to 13 kOhm at 20 °C for 2014-15 units. P0A2C means the voltage is too low, which the module reads as an impossibly hot motor: GM sets it on 2013 two-mode trucks above 230 °C (near 0 V), Type B, two trips; the 2011 table uses 184 °C, the 2013 MGU mild hybrid 236 °C.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Motor temperature shows a very high fixed value in live data
Electric drive power reduced or disabled
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Thermistor internally shorted (often only with transaxle or motor)
Chafed extension harness between drive unit and inverter
Faulty sensor input in the inverter/motor control module

P0A2D.d: With an NTC thermistor, a high signal voltage stands for a cold motor, and a voltage close to the 5 V pull-up means the circuit is open. GM sets P0A2D on its 2013 two-mode trucks when the reading falls below -40 °C, Type B over two trips; if the fault is already present at start-up it waits until the motor has warmed up under load for at least 1.5 minutes.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Motor temperature shows about -40 degrees in live data
Electric drive power limited
c: Open signal or ground wire of the motor temperature sensor
Connector unplugged or terminal pushed out, often after drive unit work
Thermistor open inside the motor or transaxle
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage

P0A2E.d: P0A2E flags short jumps or dropouts in the motor A temperature signal that are too brief or too erratic for the low/high checks. Bentley documents it for the Bentayga PHEV and Flying Spur Hybrid 2020-23: the resistance in the sensor crimp changes suddenly at high temperature, and only the sensor has to be replaced, although the engine and gearbox come out to reach it.
s: Check engine light or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Fault comes and goes, often after hard driving
Gearbox or electric drive warning on some models
c: Worn contacts in a coupling connector of the sensor line (Audi A7 e quattro)
Resistance jumps in the sensor crimp at high temperature (Bentley hybrids)
Chafed or loosely routed sensor wire with intermittent contact

P0A2F.d: Unlike its siblings, P0A2F reports a real thermal problem: the sensor works, but motor A stays too hot. GM sets it on 2013 two-mode trucks when the temperature exceeds 200 °C and does not fall below the 135 °C reset level, Type B, provided no circuit or plausibility fault is active.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Electric drive power drops sharply or is cut
Engine runs more often to support the drive
c: Motor cooling failure such as a weak pump, low fluid or blocked cooler
Sustained high load such as towing or long climbs in electric mode
Temperature sensor reading too high while still within range

P0A30.d: P0A30 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor in the second traction motor (motor B). It is meant for faults the control unit can see on the sensor line but cannot classify as too low, too high or implausible.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Reduced electric drive power
Motor B temperature missing or implausible in live data
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector between motor B and its control module
Chafed or broken sensor wiring at the drive unit
Thermistor in the motor winding failed (often only replaceable with the motor)
Faulty sensor input in the motor control module

P0A31.d: P0A31 checks whether the motor B temperature reading makes sense, typically after a long rest when all parts should be close to the same temperature. GM compares it with other temperatures: the 2011 tables flag a gap above 20 °C to the average of power-electronics coolant and transmission fluid after 6 h without propulsion (Type A); the 2013 two-mode trucks allow 28 °C against the inverter module after 360 min key-of
s: Hybrid warning light after a cold start
Motor B temperature differs clearly from other temperatures after a long rest
Electric drive limited as a precaution
c: Motor B thermistor reading drifted out of tolerance
Corroded terminals adding resistance in the sensor circuit
Comparison sensor (inverter, coolant or fluid temperature) is wrong
Uneven cooling of the drive unit, e.g. low fluid level

P0A32.d: P0A32 means the motor B temperature signal sits below its valid voltage range. GM uses an NTC thermistor, so a voltage near 0 V reads as an impossibly hot winding: the 2011 hybrid tables set it above 184 °C (Type A, one trip), the 2013 two-mode trucks above 230 °C (Type B, two trips).
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Motor B temperature shows an extremely high fixed value
Electric drive reduced or switched off
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Chafed harness between drive unit and motor control module
Faulty sensor input in the motor control module

P0A33.d: P0A33 is stored when the motor B temperature signal stays above its valid voltage range. With GM's NTC thermistor a voltage near 5 V reads as an impossibly cold motor: GM sets it below -41 °C in the 2011 tables (Type A) and below -40 °C on the 2013 two-mode trucks (Type B, two trips).
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Motor B temperature shows about -40 °C regardless of conditions
Electric drive power limited
c: Open sensor circuit or unplugged connector
Spread or corroded terminals at the motor or module connector
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P0A34.d: P0A34 covers a motor B temperature signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing permanently. A winding temperature cannot change by tens of degrees within milliseconds, so such steps point to a loose contact, a chafed wire or a cracked solder joint.
s: Hybrid warning that appears and clears on its own
Motor B temperature jumps in live data
Occasional loss of electric drive power
c: Loose or fretting terminal in the sensor connector
Wire insulation chafed through at a moving harness section
Cracked joint at the thermistor leads inside the motor

P0A35.d: Unlike the sensor codes, P0A35 reports that motor B is actually too hot according to a working sensor. GM's 2011 hybrid tables set it above 149 °C (Type A, one trip); the 2013 two-mode trucks use 200 °C, clear it only below 135 °C and run it only while P0A31 is not active (Type B).
s: Noticeable loss of electric drive power
Hybrid system overheat or warning message
Engine runs more often to compensate
c: Electric coolant pump of the drive cooling circuit failed or weak
Low coolant or transmission fluid in the motor cooling path
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked
Extended high load such as towing or long climbs

P0A36.d: P0A36 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor in the hybrid generator, the machine that is mainly driven by the engine to produce electricity. It covers faults the module detects on the sensor line without classing them as low, high or implausible.
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Generator output or battery charging restricted
Generator temperature missing or implausible in live data
c: Loose or corroded connector between generator and its control unit
Damaged sensor wiring near the transaxle
Generator coil thermistor failed (usually replaced with the generator)
Faulty input in the generator control unit

P0A37.d: P0A37 tests whether the generator temperature reading is believable. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: once per drive cycle, after at least 5,400 s of soak and with the inverter switched off, the generator W-phase coil temperature is compared with the front motor coil and with the oil temperature.
s: Hybrid warning after the first start of the day
Generator temperature differs from oil temperature after a long rest
Generator operation possibly restricted
c: Generator coil sensor reading out of tolerance
Corroded connector or damaged harness in the sensor circuit
Fault in the power drive unit that evaluates the sensor
Comparison sensor (motor coil or oil temperature) reads wrong

P0A38.d: P0A38 means the generator temperature signal has fallen below the range a healthy sensor can produce. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the voltage of the generator W-phase coil sensor is 0.1 V or less for at least 0.5 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply.
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Generator temperature shows an implausibly high fixed value
Battery charging by the engine restricted
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Damaged connector or harness between generator and power drive unit
Faulty sensor input in the power drive unit

P0A39.d: P0A39 is the high-side counterpart of P0A38: the generator temperature signal stays above the range a working sensor can deliver. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the generator W-phase coil sensor voltage reaches 4.93 V or more for at least 0.5 s.
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Generator temperature shows a very low fixed value
Generator output or series mode restricted
c: Open sensor circuit or unplugged generator connector
Spread or corroded terminals at the generator or power drive unit
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage

P0A3A.d: P0A3A flags a generator temperature signal that is interrupted or jumps only briefly. Since the thermal mass of a generator winding rules out sudden steps, such behaviour indicates a contact or wiring problem rather than a real temperature change.
s: Hybrid warning that appears now and then
Generator temperature jumps in live data
Occasionally restricted battery charging by the engine
c: Loose or fretting terminal in the generator sensor connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Harness chafed against the transaxle housing

P0A3B.d: P0A3B reports that the hybrid generator itself has become too hot, with the temperature sensor working correctly. Mitsubishi documents it as generator coil temperature high on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the monitor runs continuously and sets the code when the W-phase coil temperature criterion of 199 °C is met for one second.
s: Hybrid system warning or overheat message
Reduced charging and power when the engine drives the generator
Battery state of charge drops during driving
c: Fault in the oil cooling circuit of the generator (low oil, leak, pump)
Internal generator fault such as damaged winding insulation
Power drive unit commanding excessive generator current

P0A3C.d: P0A3C reports overheating of the inverter that powers drive motor A, usually measured at its IGBT power switches. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the front motor control unit reads 166 °C or more at the U-phase upper IGBT for 0.12 s; other switch positions have their own P30xx codes.
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Strongly reduced drive power
Coolant loss from the inverter circuit
c: PCU or inverter radiator damaged or leaking (Honda Accord/Civic Hybrid)
Internal inverter defect such as a cracked solder joint (Honda Civic Hybrid 2012-15)
Low coolant or failed electric pump in the inverter cooling circuit

P0A3D.d: P0A3D is the over-temperature code for the inverter feeding drive motor B. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV this is the rear motor control unit, and Mitsubishi sets the code when its IGBT temperature is 156 °C or higher for one second.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced rear-axle drive power
Fault appears after long climbs or high load
c: Electric water pump of the EV cooling circuit failed
Low coolant or air in the EV cooling circuit
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked
Internal fault in the rear motor and inverter assembly

P0A3E.d: P0A3E reports that the inverter controlling the hybrid generator is too hot. Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV when the generator control unit reads 156 °C or more at the U-phase IGBT for 0.12 s; the other switches report via P30AD to P30B1.
s: Several hybrid warning lights at once
Reduced hybrid system performance
Coolant loss or visible damage at the front radiator area
c: PCU radiator punctured or leaking after road debris (Honda Accord/Civic Hybrid)
Low coolant or failed electric pump in the inverter cooling circuit
Internal fault in the power drive unit

P0A3F.d: The rotor position of a traction motor is read by a resolver: one excitation coil and two pickup coils that return sine and cosine signals. P0A3F is the basic circuit code for motor A and mostly means the signal is gone.
s: Sudden loss of propulsion, sometimes normal again after a restart
MIL and hybrid/EV system warning on
Vehicle will not enter ready mode or electric drive is disabled
c: Spread or poorly seated terminal at the resolver connector (documented on the Chevrolet Bolt)
Open or shorted excitation, sine or cosine wire between motor and inverter
Low 12 V auxiliary battery voltage disturbing the motor control module (Subaru, fixed by reprogramming)
Resolver coil failed inside the motor
Faulty resolver excitation or input stage in the inverter/motor control module

P0A40.d: P0A40 means the resolver of motor A still delivers a signal, but its quality is poor or implausible. GM calls this a degraded signal: the sine or cosine value exceeds 4.0 V, judged within 0.2 to 0.4 s of a 2 s window (Type A, one trip in 2016; Type B, two trips on the 2013 mild hybrid).
s: Drive system fault message in the instrument cluster
Vehicle cannot be started or will not enter ready mode
Electric drive disabled or torque jerks while driving
c: Rotor position sensor (resolver) delivering a degraded signal, e.g. Audi G713
Worn, loose or contaminated contacts in the resolver connectors (Audi, Bentley)
Sensor wires pinched or misrouted on the gearbox housing after a repair
Faulty resolver evaluation in the inverter/motor control module

P0A41.d: P0A41 reports that a resolver signal of motor A sits below its permitted range, as happens with a sine, cosine or excitation wire shorted to ground, a shorted coil or a broken line pulled down by the input circuit. Kia documents it on the 2011-13 Optima Hybrid: an intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp with P0A41 in the motor control unit, traced to internal shorts or poor pin fit in the sub-harness between the hybr
s: Intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp
Electric drive temporarily disabled
Code returns after clearing, often with vibration or heat
c: Internal short in the resolver sub-harness between power control unit and motor (Kia Optima Hybrid)
Poor pin fit at the resolver connectors
Shorted resolver coil inside the motor
Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control unit

P0A42.d: P0A42 is the counterpart to P0A41: a resolver line of motor A reads above its allowed range. Typical triggers are a sine, cosine or excitation wire shorted to a supply voltage, or an open coil whose line is pulled up by the bias resistors of the input circuit, which drives the converter into clipping.
s: Intermittent MIL or hybrid service lamp
Electric drive disabled or vehicle not ready
Reduced power until the fault clears
c: Resolver wire shorted to a supply voltage inside the sub-harness (Kia Optima Hybrid)
Open sine or cosine line pulled high by the input circuit
Poor pin fit or corrosion at the resolver connectors
Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control unit

P0A43.d: P0A43 is set when the motor A resolver signal drops out or jumps only briefly, so that neither a steady low, high nor a lasting loss is confirmed. Stellantis uses it on the Pacifica Hybrid: NHTSA files show P0A43-00 stored in the hybrid control processor next to P0A3F and P0A45, and a 2026 parts review tells dealers to check active bulletins and flash the hybrid control processor before ordering a new power inverter
s: Hybrid system warning or MIL that comes and goes
Brief loss of propulsion, normal again after restart
Code stored as history without current symptoms
c: Loose or spread terminal in the resolver connector, losing contact under vibration
Hybrid control or inverter software needing an update (Stellantis)
Chafed resolver wiring making intermittent contact
Intermittent fault in the power inverter module

P0A44.d: P0A44 reports that the speed derived from the motor A resolver is above the highest speed the motor may run. Mitsubishi uses it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV front motor: set at 15,500 rpm or more for 0.5 s with module supply above 8 V, judged only when the position sensor itself is fault-free; the guided fix after other codes are ruled out is a new front motor.
s: Electric drive torque cut during acceleration or high speed
Hybrid/EV system warning and MIL
Reduced top speed in limp mode
c: Mechanical fault in the front motor or its drivetrain (Mitsubishi replaces the motor)
Real overspeed from wheel spin or a slipping coupling
Disturbed resolver signal producing a false speed value
Motor control module calculating speed incorrectly

P0A45.d: P0A45 is the general circuit code for the resolver of the second traction motor (B), usually meaning its signal is missing. GM sets it like P0A3F when sine or cosine amplitude falls below 2.3 V (Type A, one trip).
s: MIL and hybrid system warning message
Loss of rear-axle electric drive or all-wheel drive
Reduced power or vehicle not ready
c: Damaged or faulty frame/body wire harness to the rear motor (Toyota RAV4 Hybrid)
Poor contact at the motor B resolver connector
Resolver or control unit inside the rear motor assembly failed (Mitsubishi)
Hybrid control software needing an update (Stellantis)

P0A46.d: P0A46 reports that the motor B resolver still delivers a signal, but one that is degraded or not plausible. GM uses the same check as P0A40 for its second motor: sine or cosine above 4.0 V, with a failure counted when it persists for 0.2 to 0.4 s of a 2 s window (Type A, one trip in the 2011 and 2016 tables).
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Rear or second motor disabled, reduced traction or power
Jerky torque delivery before the fault sets
c: Resolver of motor B delivering unequal or distorted sine/cosine signals
High contact resistance or moisture in the resolver connector
Fault inside the rear motor assembly incl. bearing damage (Mitsubishi)
Damaged shielding letting inverter noise into the resolver lines

P0A47.d: P0A47 means a resolver signal of motor B is below its allowed range, typically from a sine, cosine or excitation line shorted to ground or a shorted coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: MIL or hybrid service lamp
Second motor disabled, reduced traction or power
Fault may come and go with vibration or moisture
c: Resolver sine, cosine or excitation line shorted to ground
Poor pin fit or water ingress at the motor B resolver connector
Shorted resolver coil inside motor B
Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control module

P0A48.d: P0A48 reports a motor B resolver line reading above its allowed range, for example a sine, cosine or excitation wire shorted to a supply voltage, or an open coil whose line is pulled up by the input bias circuit until the converter clips. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Second motor disabled, reduced traction or power
Vehicle may not enter ready mode
c: Resolver line shorted to a supply voltage
Open sine or cosine line pulled high by the input circuit
Corroded or loose terminals at the motor B resolver connector
Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control module

P0A49.d: P0A49 covers short dropouts or jumps in the motor B resolver signal that are too brief to count as a lasting loss, low or high fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hybrid warning or MIL that comes and goes
Brief loss of second-motor drive, often over bumps
Code stored as history without current symptoms
c: Loose or spread terminal in the motor B resolver connector
Chafed or stretched resolver wiring near the rear axle or subframe
Moisture in the connector causing intermittent leakage
Hybrid control software needing an update

P0A4A.d: P0A4A reports that the speed calculated from the motor B resolver exceeds the motor's permitted maximum. Mitsubishi uses it for the rear motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV: set at 12,500 rpm or more for at least 1 s with supply above 8 V, and only judged once the rear position sensor codes P0A45, P0A46, P0C57, P0C58, P0C61 and P0C62 are ruled out; otherwise the rear motor assembly is replaced, bearing damage being one
s: Rear electric drive shut off, front-wheel drive only
Hybrid/EV warning and MIL
Reduced acceleration in limp mode
c: Fault in the rear motor assembly, e.g. damaged bearing or control unit (Mitsubishi)
Real overspeed from rear wheel spin on low grip
Disturbed resolver signal producing a false speed value

P0A4B.d: P0A4B covers the resolver that tells the inverter where the generator rotor stands; without a valid angle the generator cannot be commutated. Mitsubishi (Outlander PHEV 2023) runs the check continuously once the generator control unit has at least 8.0 V and sets P0A4B when its internal status flags stay failed for 0.23 s or 0.28 s; low and high signal levels go to separate codes there.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Engine does not start or crank in hybrid mode
Electric drive or charging by the generator disabled
c: False detection in the inverter monitor software (Volvo, fixed by update)
Damaged resolver wiring or connector between generator and inverter
Resolver evaluation in the power drive unit faulty

P0A4C.d: P0A4C means the generator resolver delivers signals that are electrically present but implausible, so the computed rotor angle cannot be trusted. Mitsubishi documents the exact limits for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the sine or cosine winding voltage must stay between 2.1 and 2.9 V; if either leaves that window for 0.28 s, or an internal status fault persists for 0.31 s, the generator control unit stores P0A4C.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced drive power or engine-only operation
Engine start via the generator not possible
c: Damaged shielding letting interference onto the sine/cosine lines
Resolver winding drifted out of tolerance
Faulty resolver input stage in the power drive unit

P0A4D.d: P0A4D reports a generator resolver signal stuck below its permitted range, as caused by a sine, cosine or excitation line shorted to ground or a winding short. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Generator disabled, engine-only or no-start condition
c: Sine, cosine or excitation line shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the resolver connector
Shorted resolver winding inside the generator

P0A4E.d: P0A4E is set when a generator resolver signal sits above its permitted range, which usually points to an open signal line pulled up by the input circuit or a short to a supply voltage. No manufacturer documents P0A4E publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Generator disabled, engine-only or no-start condition
c: Open resolver signal line or pushed-out terminal
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty resolver input stage in the power drive unit

P0A4F.d: P0A4F flags a generator resolver signal that drops out or jumps briefly and then recovers, as opposed to a steady fault. No manufacturer documents P0A4F publicly.
s: Hybrid warning that appears and clears again
Short loss of electric drive or jerky power delivery
Fault often linked to bumps or heat
c: Loose or fretting terminals in the resolver connectors
Chafed resolver cable that breaks contact under vibration
Heat-related cracks in wiring or solder joints

P0A50.d: P0A50 says the generator speed derived from its resolver has exceeded the permitted maximum. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with at least 8.0 V at the generator control unit and the position sensor itself judged healthy, a speed of 15,500 rpm or more lasting 0.5 s stores P0A50, and the repair path ends with replacing the generator.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Generator shut off, reduced power or engine-only drive
c: Internal generator fault (Mitsubishi repair path ends with generator replacement)
Mechanical fault in the transaxle or clutch letting the generator overrun
Incorrect speed calculation in the power drive unit

P0A51.d: P0A51 reports a fault in the circuit of the current sensor that measures the phase current of drive motor A. The inverter needs this value for torque control and overcurrent protection.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Drive motor A disabled, vehicle may not move or runs on engine only
c: Current sensor in the inverter assembly failed
Sensor supply or signal line interrupted inside the inverter
Evaluation circuit on the motor control board faulty

P0A52.d: P0A52 means the current sensor of drive motor A delivers values that are electrically valid but do not fit the operating state. Typical checks compare the reading at zero current with its expected offset, or compare redundant sensors with each other.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced or jerky electric drive
Drive motor A disabled, engine-only operation
c: Sensor offset drifted beyond the compensation range
Control and monitoring sensor disagree due to one degraded sensor
Electrical interference or poor ground on the sensor signal

P0A53.d: P0A53 is stored when the current sensor signal of drive motor A stays below its valid range, typically from a signal line shorted to ground, a lost sensor supply or a failed Hall element. No manufacturer documents P0A53 publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
High-voltage system switched off, vehicle may not move
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Hall element of the current sensor failed

P0A54.d: P0A54 signals that the current sensor output of drive motor A sits above its valid range, as caused by an open ground, a short to the sensor supply or an internal sensor fault that saturates the output. No manufacturer documents P0A54 publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Drive motor A disabled or power strongly reduced
c: Open ground of the current sensor
Signal line shorted to the sensor supply
Internal sensor fault with saturated output

P0A55.d: P0A55 is the general circuit fault of the current sensor that measures the current of drive motor B, typically the second traction motor, for example on a rear axle. The inverter needs this signal for torque control and to protect its power switches.
s: Hybrid or electric drive warning with MIL
Drive motor B disabled, loss of electric all-wheel drive or reduced power
c: Current sensor of drive motor B failed (usually inside the inverter)
Sensor supply or signal line interrupted or shorted
Evaluation circuit on the motor B control board faulty

P0A56.d: P0A56 means the current sensor of drive motor B delivers electrically valid values that do not match the operating state, for example a zero-current offset outside its band or a reading that disagrees with a redundant sensor. No manufacturer documents P0A56 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Reduced or missing drive from motor B
c: Current sensor offset drifted or offset learning disturbed
Current sensor of drive motor B degraded
Electrical interference on the sensor signal

P0A57.d: P0A57 is set when the signal of the drive motor B current sensor stays below its valid range, usually from a signal line shorted to ground, a missing sensor supply or a failed Hall element. No manufacturer documents P0A57 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Drive motor B or the whole high-voltage system switched off
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Hall element of the current sensor failed

P0A58.d: P0A58 reports that the output of the drive motor B current sensor sits above its valid range, for instance from an open sensor ground, a short to the sensor supply or an internal fault that saturates the output. No manufacturer documents P0A58 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Drive motor B disabled, reduced power
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal line shorted to the sensor supply

P0A59.d: P0A59 is the general circuit fault of the current sensor on the hybrid generator, the electric machine driven by the engine that charges the battery and often starts the engine. Its inverter uses the current reading to control generator torque.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine runs constantly or the high-voltage battery is no longer charged
Vehicle may not enter ready mode
c: Generator current sensor failed (usually inside the inverter)
Sensor supply or signal line interrupted or shorted
Evaluation circuit on the generator control board faulty

P0A5A.d: P0A5A means the generator current sensor delivers values that are electrically valid but implausible, for example a wrong zero offset or phase currents that no longer add up. No hybrid manufacturer documents P0A5A publicly with criteria.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Reduced charging or engine running more often
c: Generator current sensor offset drifted or offset learning disturbed
Control module calibration requiring an update

P0A5B.d: P0A5B indicates that the signal of the generator current sensor stays below its valid range, as caused by a signal line shorted to ground, a lost sensor supply or a failed sensing element. No hybrid manufacturer documents P0A5B publicly with criteria.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
High-voltage system switched off or battery no longer charged
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Sensing element of the generator current sensor failed

P0A5C.d: P0A5C means the generator current sensor output lies above its valid range, typically from an open sensor ground, a short to the sensor supply or a saturated sensor. No hybrid manufacturer documents P0A5C publicly with criteria.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Generator disabled, engine start or battery charging affected
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal line shorted to the sensor supply
Generator current sensor with saturated output

P0A5D.d: P0A5D concerns the current in phase U of drive motor A, as seen by the inverter. Audi documents it on the 2021-23 Q5 e quattro (bulletin 2069917/1): P0A5D00, often with P0A6000 and P0A6300, is stored in the electric drive control module J841, the cluster reads Drive system: fault and the car may not start or drive.
s: Drive system fault message and MIL
Vehicle does not start or the drive system cannot be activated
c: High-voltage phase cable or weld joint to drive motor A faulty (Audi Q5 e quattro)
Phase current sensor in the inverter failed
Winding fault in phase U of drive motor A

P0A5E.d: P0A5E means too little current flows, or is sensed, in phase U of drive motor A, the classic sign of an open phase. GM describes the check for the motor control processor of the 2016 Chevrolet Volt and in its 2018 hybrid tables: with the inverter in normal PWM above 50 V and a squared current command above 900 A2 (2016) or 4,900 A2 (2018), the absolute U current is sampled while the rotor is within 30 degrees of the
s: MIL and propulsion system warning
Rough or reduced electric drive, possible engine-only operation
c: Open circuit in the phase U cable, connector or terminal
Phase U current sensor reads zero
Phase U switch of the inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase U in drive motor A

P0A5F.d: P0A5F reports excessive current in phase U of drive motor A, a condition the inverter treats as overcurrent. Hyundai documents it on the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid (bulletin 17-01-057-1, campaign T2J): coolant leaking inside the traction motor set the Check Engine and hybrid lights with P0A5F, P0A62 or P0A65, often together with the isolation fault P0AA6; drivers noticed weak acceleration and a dead air conditioner.
s: Check Engine and hybrid warning lights
Reduced power when accelerating
Air conditioning inoperative (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
c: Internal coolant leak in the traction motor causing insulation breakdown (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
Shorted winding or phase lead of drive motor A
Inverter power stage fault in phase U

P0A60.d: P0A60 covers the current in phase V of drive motor A. Toyota uses it with sub codes: a field report filed with NHTSA describes a 2006 Highlander Hybrid whose master warning lit and which would not move; P0A60 sub code 501 had set first, followed by P0A63, P0A78 and P0AEF, all returning at once after clearing, and the inverter assembly was replaced.
s: Master warning or drive system fault message, MIL
Vehicle will not move or start
c: Internal fault in the inverter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
High-voltage phase V cable or weld joint faulty (Audi Q5 e quattro)
Winding fault in phase V of drive motor A

P0A61.d: P0A61 indicates that phase V of drive motor A carries, or reports, too little current when it should be near its peak, pointing to an open phase V circuit. GM uses the same peak-axis test as for phase U on the 2016 Chevrolet Volt motor control processor and in its 2018 hybrid tables, here with the rotor within 30 degrees of the V phase axis: inverter above 50 V in normal PWM, squared current command above 900 A2 in 2
s: MIL and propulsion system warning
Jerky or weak electric drive
c: Open circuit in the phase V cable, connector or terminal
Phase V current sensor reads zero
Phase V switch of the inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase V in drive motor A

P0A62.d: P0A62 signals overcurrent in phase V of drive motor A. Hyundai lists it in bulletin 17-01-057-1 for the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid next to P0A5F, P0A65 and the isolation fault P0AA6: the bulletin traces them to coolant leaking inside the traction motor and checks the high-voltage insulation first.
s: Check Engine and hybrid warning lights
Weak acceleration, air conditioning inoperative
c: Coolant inside the traction motor with loss of insulation (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
Phase V lead or winding shorted to ground or to another phase
Inverter power stage fault in phase V

P0A63.d: P0A63 concerns the current in phase W of drive motor A. In the Toyota field reports filed with NHTSA it always appears beside P0A60: on a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with sub code 502, after P0A60 sub code 501, together with P0A78 and P0AEF, master warning on and no drive; the inverter assembly was replaced.
s: Master warning or drive system fault message, MIL
Vehicle will not move or start
c: Internal fault in the inverter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
High-voltage phase W cable or weld joint faulty (Audi Q5 e quattro)

P0A64.d: P0A64 means phase W of drive motor A shows too little current at the moment it should peak, typically an open W lead or a W sensor stuck at zero. GM completes its three-phase sequence with this code on the 2016 Chevrolet Volt motor control processor and in the 2018 hybrid tables: when the rotor sits within 30 degrees of the W phase axis, the inverter runs normal PWM above 50 V and the squared current command exceeds
s: MIL and propulsion system warning
Uneven or reduced electric drive torque
c: Open circuit in the phase W cable, connector or terminal
Phase W current sensor reads zero
Phase W switch of the inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase W in drive motor A

P0A65.d: P0A65 reports overcurrent in phase W of drive motor A. It is the third phase code in Hyundai bulletin 17-01-057-1 for the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid, campaign T2J: with an internal coolant leak in the traction motor, P0A65, P0A5F or P0A62 set with Check Engine and hybrid lights, often joined by the isolation fault P0AA6.
s: Check Engine and hybrid warning lights
Reduced power when accelerating
Air conditioning inoperative (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
c: Internal coolant leak in the traction motor (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
Phase W lead or winding shorted to ground or to another phase
Inverter power stage fault in phase W

P0A66.d: P0A66 is the general fault code for the current in phase U of drive motor B, the second electric machine of a two-motor hybrid or an electric rear-axle motor. No manufacturer documents P0A66 publicly; GM, for instance, only uses the open-phase code P0A67 for this phase.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Motor B switched off, less power or no electric all-wheel drive
c: Phase U current sensor of motor B failed (inside the inverter)
Phase U high-voltage cable or terminal between inverter and motor B faulty
Internal fault in the motor B power stage
Winding fault in phase U of drive motor B

P0A67.d: P0A67 reports that phase U of drive motor B carries too little current at the moment it should peak, which GM interprets as an open circuit in that phase. In the 2016 Chevrolet Volt tables for motor control processor B the test runs while the rotor is within 30 degrees of the U axis, the inverter is above 50 V in normal PWM and the squared current command exceeds 900 A²; a peak below 9 A for 0.4 s within a 0.6 s wind
s: MIL on the first trip and propulsion system warning
Jerky or weak electric drive, reduced power
c: Open circuit in the phase U cable, connector or terminal of motor B
Phase U switch of the motor B inverter not conducting
Phase U current sensor stuck at zero
Open winding of phase U in drive motor B

P0A68.d: P0A68 means the current measured in phase U of drive motor B rises above its plausible maximum, either because a real overcurrent flows, for example through damaged insulation, a winding short or a shorted power switch, or because the phase sensor reads too high. No manufacturer documents P0A68 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL, often with an insulation fault code
Sudden loss of drive from motor B
c: Winding short or insulation breakdown in phase U of motor B (e.g. coolant ingress)
Shorted power switch in the phase U leg of the inverter
Phase U current sensor reading too high (gain or offset fault)

P0A69.d: P0A69 flags a general fault in the current of phase V of drive motor B. No manufacturer documents P0A69 publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced power, motor B no longer contributes
c: Phase V current sensor of motor B failed
Fault on the motor B inverter board or power stage
Phase V high-voltage cable or terminal loose or damaged

P0A6A.d: P0A6A is GM's open-circuit test for phase V of drive motor B. The controller checks each phase on its own as the rotor turns; for phase V it looks at the window of 30 degrees either side of the V axis, where the current should be largest.
s: MIL and propulsion system warning after the first trip
Vibration or uneven torque from motor B before shutdown
c: Phase V lead, connector or bolted terminal of motor B open
Phase V switch of the motor B inverter not switching
Phase V current sensor output stuck at zero
Open phase V winding in motor B

P0A6B.d: P0A6B is stored when phase V of drive motor B reports more current than the operating state allows. No manufacturer documents P0A6B publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Motor B cut out, reduced acceleration
c: Phase V current sensor gain or offset drifted high
Shorted power switch in the phase V leg
Winding or insulation fault in phase V of motor B

P0A6C.d: P0A6C covers a general fault in the phase W current of drive motor B. No manufacturer documents P0A6C publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Loss of electric drive on the axle driven by motor B
c: Phase W high-voltage lead or terminal to motor B damaged or loose
Internal fault of the motor B inverter

P0A6D.d: P0A6D completes GM's set of open-phase tests for drive motor B with phase W. Because each phase is only judged while the rotor sits within 30 degrees of its own axis, the code points to W alone rather than to the motor as a whole.
s: MIL on the first trip with propulsion warning
Rough or reduced electric drive
c: Phase W lead or terminal of motor B interrupted
Phase W switch of the inverter not conducting
Phase W current sensor stuck at zero
Open phase W winding in motor B

P0A6E.d: P0A6E indicates excessive current, measured or real, in phase W of drive motor B. No manufacturer documents P0A6E publicly.
s: MIL and hybrid warning, possibly with an isolation fault
Motor B no longer drives; possible air conditioning shutdown
c: Insulation breakdown or winding short in phase W (moisture, coolant)
Shorted switch in the phase W leg of the inverter
Phase W current sensor reading too high

P0A6F.d: P0A6F is the general fault code for the phase U current of the hybrid generator, the motor-generator that is mainly driven by the engine, starts it and charges the battery, such as Toyota's MG1 or Hyundai's hybrid starter-generator. No manufacturer documents P0A6F publicly; Toyota's published field reports show generator codes for phases V and W only.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Engine cannot be started electrically or battery is no longer charged
c: Generator phase U current sensor failed
Fault in the generator section of the inverter assembly
Generator phase U cable or terminal faulty

P0A70.d: P0A70 means phase U of the hybrid generator carries or reports too little current while the generator is loaded, typical of an open phase or a sensor stuck near zero. No manufacturer documents P0A70 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine runs rough at start or battery charge level keeps dropping
c: Open circuit in the generator phase U lead or terminal
Generator phase U current sensor stuck near zero
Phase U switch in the generator inverter not conducting

P0A71.d: P0A71 is set when the current in phase U of the hybrid generator exceeds its permitted level. No manufacturer documents P0A71 publicly.
s: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL
Hybrid system shuts down; vehicle may not move or restart
c: Shorted power switch in the generator phase U leg
Winding or insulation short in generator phase U
Faulty phase U current sensor or its evaluation in the inverter

P0A72.d: P0A72 reports a fault in the phase V current of the hybrid generator. Toyota uses it: a field report filed with NHTSA covers a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with the MIL on and P0A72 stored together with P0A75 for generator phase W, P0A60 and P0A63 for drive motor A, and inverter performance codes including P0A78; after checking connector fit and the resistance of the three-phase cables, the inverter/converter assembly was
s: MIL and master warning, several hybrid codes at once
Vehicle may not move or enter ready mode
c: Internal fault in the inverter/converter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
Generator phase V current sensor failed
Poor pin fit or damaged three-phase cable to the generator

P0A73.d: P0A73 indicates that phase V of the hybrid generator delivers or reports too little current under load. No manufacturer documents P0A73 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine runs more often, battery charge does not recover
c: Generator phase V current sensor reading near zero
Generator phase V lead or terminal open
Phase V switch in the generator inverter not conducting

P0A74.d: P0A74 appears when phase V of the hybrid generator shows more current than its limit allows. No manufacturer documents P0A74 publicly.
s: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL
Hybrid system shutdown, possibly no propulsion
c: Phase V sensor offset drifted or offset correction failed
Power switch in the generator phase V leg not turning off
Winding or insulation short in generator phase V

P0A75.d: P0A75 stands for a fault in the phase W current of the hybrid generator. Toyota documents it in practice: in a field report from an NHTSA investigation of 2006 Highlander Hybrid inverters, P0A75 appeared next to P0A72, the drive motor phase codes P0A60 and P0A63 and inverter performance codes, and the root cause was inside the inverter/converter, which was replaced.
s: MIL and master warning, usually with other hybrid codes
Vehicle will not become ready or will not move
c: Internal fault in the inverter/converter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
Generator phase W current sensor failed
Generator phase W cable or connector faulty

P0A76.d: P0A76 signals that phase W of the hybrid generator conducts or reports too little current while the generator should be producing or absorbing torque. No manufacturer documents P0A76 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine start harsh or delayed, charging reduced
c: Loose terminal, cracked lead or corroded connector in generator phase W
Generator phase W current sensor stuck near zero
Open phase W winding in the generator

P0A77.d: P0A77 is the excess-current code for phase W of the hybrid generator. No manufacturer documents P0A77 publicly.
s: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL
Hybrid system shuts down during charging or engine start
c: Turn-to-turn short or insulation breakdown in generator phase W
Power switch in the generator phase W leg failed closed
Generator phase W current sensor with excessive gain

P0A78.d: P0A78 means the inverter stage feeding drive motor A has reported a power-switch fault. GM explains the check in its hybrid OBD tables: the IGBT module watches each phase for desaturation, a sign of a short between the upper and lower switch; if that status persists for about 2 ms the code sets as Type A, MIL on the first trip.
s: MIL and hybrid or high-voltage warning
No electric drive, engine-only operation
Stop safely warning on some models
c: IGBT desaturation or short in the inverter power stage
Power inverter module defective (replaced on Jeep Wrangler 4xe)
Shorted winding or phase cable of drive motor A

P0A79.d: P0A79 is the drive motor B counterpart of P0A78: the inverter stage for motor B has detected a power-switch fault. In GM hybrid OBD tables the IGBT module reports a desaturation status on a high or low side switch of any phase; persisting for about 2 ms it sets P0A79 as Type A with MIL on the first trip.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
No electric drive, engine-only operation
Loss of propulsion in severe cases
c: IGBT desaturation or short in the motor B power stage
Loose high-voltage cable at the inverter terminal (Pacifica Hybrid)

P0A7A.d: P0A7A reports that the inverter stage driving the generator has signalled a fault, for example overcurrent or a failed power switch. Toyota uses the code across its hybrids and splits it with information codes.
s: MIL, master warning and Check Hybrid System message
Reduced power or vehicle will not enter ready mode
c: Internal generator inverter fault with overcurrent (Toyota information code 122)
Fault in the generator inside the transaxle
Insufficient inverter cooling stressing the power stage

P0A7B.d: P0A7B is a request code: the battery energy control module, which has found an emissions-relevant fault of its own, asks the engine control module to switch on the MIL, and the engine controller stores P0A7B. The actual cause sits in a separate code in the battery module.
s: MIL on
Additional codes stored in the battery control module
c: Emissions-relevant fault stored in the battery energy control module
Air trapped at the battery coolant pump (Corvette E-Ray, with P0E3C)
Frozen power supply relay of the drive motor control module (Subaru Crosstrek Hybrid)

P0A7C.d: P0A7C reports that the electronics controlling the hybrid motors, mainly the inverter, have run hotter than allowed. Ford uses the code on its hybrids and stores it in the PCM.
s: Wrench or hybrid warning light
Reduced power, especially under high load or heat
c: Coolant pump of the motor electronics cooling loop failed
Low coolant or air in the electronics cooling loop
PCM calibration triggering the code without real overheating (Ford Fusion Hybrid)
Blocked electronics radiator or faulty cooling fan

P0A7D.d: The battery controller watches whether the traction or mild-hybrid pack stays inside its usable state-of-charge (SOC) window. GM sets P0A7D (Type B, two trips) when SOC stays below a program threshold (30 % or 10.5 %) for more than half of a drive cycle longer than 50 km, after allowing generator time to recover.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
No electric driving or reduced motor assist
Engine runs longer to recharge the pack
Vehicle may not start or reach ready mode
c: Pack discharged by long standing time or repeated crank/no-start attempts
Generator, DC/DC or charging path not replenishing the pack
48 V battery in low-voltage protection state (relays open)

P0A7E.d: The pack controller compares the hottest module temperature with a protection limit. GM sets P0A7E, mostly as Type A (MIL after one trip), when the maximum module temperature exceeds a program limit between about 61 and 73.5 °C, unless a temperature sensor fault is active.
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric assist and regeneration
Auto start-stop no longer works
In rare cases warning with no-start
c: Battery cooling fan inoperative or intake/filter clogged
Battery controller software logic (update released by Subaru, Porsche)
Low 12 V system voltage stopping the cooling fan
Aged cells with high internal resistance heating up

P0A7F.d: This is the state-of-health monitor that CARB requires for hybrid storage systems. GM compares the calculated pack power capability with an end-of-life table at mid state of charge and sets P0A7F as Type B (two trips) when it falls short.
s: Check engine or hybrid/IMA warning light
Weak acceleration assist, especially from a stop
Engine runs more often, higher fuel consumption
Shorter electric range on plug-in models
c: Pack capacity or power capability lost through ageing
Dust or debris in the battery cooling fan or filter overheating cells
Battery controller software misjudging health (Honda, Mercedes)
Individual weak modules pulling the pack down

P0A80.d: The battery controller has concluded that the pack is at end of life. In GM tables this is a resistance test: the maximum cell or pack resistance, measured from current and voltage swings, exceeds a temperature-dependent end-of-life threshold, and the code sets as Type A after one trip.
s: Check engine and hybrid system warning on
Noticeably weaker electric assist
Higher fuel consumption, engine runs more
c: Cell or module resistance above end-of-life limit
Clogged battery cooling fan or intake filter (Toyota)
Controller software misreading a replaced pack (Honda Accord Hybrid 2018)

P0A81.d: The controller watches the output that drives battery cooling fan 1 for an open circuit. In the 2016 GM table the fan is commanded at low duty (under 10 %) and the circuit voltage sits between about 1.6 and 5.85 V instead of being pulled low; 16 failures in 20 samples set it as Type B.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning, often no other complaint
Battery cooling fan does not run when commanded
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions
c: Fan motor or its internal electronics open
Loose or corroded fan connector, broken control wire
Faulty output stage in the battery control module

P0A82.d: This code covers a fan 1 that is electrically intact but does not deliver the requested cooling, up to standing still. No manufacturer publishes code-exact criteria; CARB requires a functional check of battery cooling where feasible.
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Fan audibly weak or silent under load
Reduced electric assist in warm weather
c: Dust or debris on fan blades or in the duct
Clogged or covered battery air intake or filter
Worn or seized fan motor bearings

P0A83.d: P0A83 means battery cooling fan 1 keeps turning although the controller has switched it off. No manufacturer publicly documents this exact code.
s: Battery fan heard running with the vehicle off or idle
Discharged 12 V battery after parking
Hybrid or check engine warning
c: Fan control wire shorted to supply voltage
Welded fan relay keeps power applied
Fan's internal speed controller ignores off command
Battery control module output stuck active

P0A84.d: The controller detects a short to ground on the control output of battery cooling fan 1. GM tests it while the fan is commanded at low duty: a circuit voltage below about 0.26 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples at 250 ms set a Type B code (MIL after two trips).
s: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan does not follow commands
Reduced hybrid power when the pack gets warm
c: Fan control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Internal short in the fan's control input
Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector
Defective output stage in the controller
