P0A85.d: The controller detects a short to voltage on the control output of battery cooling fan 1. GM runs the test while the fan is commanded between 11 % and 100 % duty: a circuit voltage above 9 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples set a Type B code with MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery fan runs constantly or not at all
Possible 12 V battery drain when parked
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Fan control input internally open or shorted to its supply
Corroded connector creating leakage to supply

P0A86.d: The 14 volt power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network of a hybrid or electric vehicle from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the Accessory Power Module (APM). Current sensor A measures the current flowing through this converter.
s: Hybrid or charging system warning lamp on
12 V battery discharges, low-voltage warnings
Possibly no other noticeable change in driving
c: Current sensor inside the 14 V power module faulty (usually not replaceable separately)
Damaged wiring or corroded connector between module and hybrid controller
Software fault in the module or hybrid controller

P0A87.d: This code means the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter, GM: APM) delivers values that are electrically valid but implausible. GM's 2016 eAssist tables (hybrid control processor HPC1) describe a stuck-in-range test: once per key cycle, while the high-voltage contactors are open and then move to precharge, the converter should be off, so the averaged input current must be near zero.
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Usually no driveability change
Possible reduced 12 V charging if the converter is limited
c: Current sensor zero-point drift inside the power module
Converter actually conducting current when it should be off (internal module fault)
Ground or reference fault distorting the sensor signal

P0A88.d: P0A88 reports that the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter feeding the 12 V system) reads too low while the converter should be delivering power. GM documents it for the Accessory Power Module: in the 2013 eAssist tables the input current must stay below 0.5 A for 1.5 s within a 2 s window while calculated output power is 0.25 to 1.5 kW; the 2016 tables use 0.50 A or less in 640 of 800 samples, e
s: MIL and hybrid/charging warning
12 V battery not charged properly
Start/stop function may be disabled
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground or open
Current sensor in the power module failed

P0A89.d: P0A89 is set when the current sensor of the 14 V power module reports more current than the converter can physically carry. GM's eAssist tables show how: in 2013 the APM input current reading had to exceed 22.5 A for 1.5 s while calculated output power was 1.5 kW or less; in 2016 the limit is 45.25 A or more in 200 of 250 samples (about 5 s) with the APM commanded on and 9 to 32 V supply.
s: MIL and hybrid/charging warning
Converter output limited, 12 V voltage drops
Start/stop function may be disabled
c: Sensor signal shorted to supply voltage
Current sensor in the power module failed
Open sensor ground pulling the signal high

P0A8A.d: P0A8A covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal of the current sensor in the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that charges the 12 V battery in hybrids and EVs. The signal is valid most of the time but briefly leaves its range or changes faster than physically possible.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional 12 V voltage fluctuations
c: Loose or fretted terminals at the module connector
Chafed wiring with intermittent short or open
Intermittent internal fault of the current sensor

P0A8B.d: The 14 V power module (DC/DC converter) regulates the voltage of the 12 V network in hybrid and electric vehicles. P0A8B is the general code for a fault in the voltage this module produces or senses, without the more specific labels unstable, low, high or performance (P0A8C to P0A8F).
s: Charging or hybrid system warning
Electrical consumers behave erratically
12 V battery discharged
c: Internal fault of the DC/DC converter
Loose or corroded 12 V output cable or ground connection
Weak 12 V battery distorting the system voltage

P0A8C.d: P0A8C indicates that the output voltage of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter supplying the 12 V network of a hybrid or EV, fluctuates beyond what the control strategy accepts instead of settling at its target. Possible reasons include a poor 12 V connection, an aged 12 V battery that no longer buffers the network, or a regulation problem inside the converter.
s: Flickering lights or display resets
Charging or hybrid system warning
Start/stop disabled
c: Loose or corroded 12 V battery terminal or ground strap
Aged 12 V battery no longer buffering the network
Unstable regulation inside the DC/DC converter

P0A8D.d: P0A8D reports too low a voltage at the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter feeding the 12 V network). GM uses it in its 2013 eAssist tables as the circuit-low check of the APM low-voltage sensor: if that sensor reads below 1 V for 1.5 s within a 2 s window while ignition voltage is 9 to 32 V, the code sets; it passes again above 1.5 V.
s: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
12 V battery discharges
Start/stop disabled
c: Voltage sense line open or shorted to ground
Voltage sensor inside the power module failed
Converter not delivering output (fuse, output cable)

P0A8E.d: P0A8E signals too high a voltage at the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter supplying the 12 V side. In GM's 2013 eAssist tables it is the circuit-high check of the APM low-voltage sensor: a reading above 20 V for 1.5 s within a 2 s window, with ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, sets the code, and it passes below 19.5 V.
s: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
Very bright lights or failing bulbs if overvoltage is real
Converter may be shut down
c: Voltage sense line shorted to a higher potential
Voltage sensor inside the power module failed
Converter regulating its output too high

P0A8F.d: P0A8F means the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter for the 12 V network) does not perform as expected even though its signals are electrically in range. GM's 2013 eAssist tables use it as a correlation test: with the APM commanded on and ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, the APM's own low-voltage reading and the run/crank voltage measured by the controller must agree within 4.5 V.
s: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
Low or fluctuating 12 V voltage
c: High resistance in 12 V output cable, fuse link or ground
Drifting voltage sensor in the module
Converter unable to hold its target voltage

P0A90.d: P0A90 reports that electric drive motor A does not behave as commanded. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the motor/generator is belt-driven from the crankshaft, so GM uses P0A90 to detect a slipping or broken belt: the motor speed is compared with the engine speed.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Belt squeal or auto-stop/start not working
Reduced electric assist or limp mode
c: Slipping, worn or broken drive belt on belt-driven motor/generators
Faulty belt tensioner or contamination on the belt
Motor, position sensor or inverter fault in full hybrids

P0A91.d: P0A91 is set when the second electric drive motor (motor B) of a hybrid or electric vehicle does not deliver the expected speed or torque, although no electrical circuit fault is detected. Motor B exists only on systems with two traction motors, such as power-split or dual-motor layouts.
s: Hybrid/EV system warning and MIL
Reduced power or limp mode
c: Inverter B fault limiting motor current
Mechanical damage to motor B or its gearing

P0A92.d: P0A92 indicates that the generator of a hybrid system, the electric machine mainly used to convert engine power into electrical energy, does not reach the expected output, speed or torque. CARB requires manufacturers to describe how they monitor the generator so that faults preventing it from working are detected.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Limp home (turtle) lamp, reduced power
Reduced charging of the high-voltage battery
c: Hybrid controller or inverter software needing update (documented by FCA)
Internal generator fault (winding, bearing, position sensor)

P0A93.d: The power inverter of a hybrid has its own coolant circuit with an electric pump, radiator and fan, separate from engine cooling. P0A93 is set when this circuit does not cool as intended.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
No EV mode, reduced power
Vehicle may not start or may stall
c: Electric inverter coolant pump failed or seized
Low coolant or air in the inverter circuit
Pump wiring, fuse or relay fault
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked

P0A94.d: P0A94 reports that a DC/DC converter in the high-voltage system does not perform as commanded. In Toyota hybrids this is the boost converter inside the inverter assembly, which raises the battery voltage before it reaches the motor inverters.
s: MIL, hybrid system and other warning lamps
Fail-safe mode with greatly reduced power
Vehicle may stop and not restart
c: Damaged power transistors in the boost converter / inverter assembly
Thermal stress from insufficient inverter cooling
Outstanding recall or software update not performed

P0A95.d: P0A95 means the battery management detects that a fuse in the high-voltage circuit has opened, usually by comparing the voltage before and after the fuse. Several makers document it: Jaguar for the I-PACE battery energy control module, where a shorted high-voltage auxiliary component blows fuses in the junction box and battery module; Porsche for the Taycan as the main high-voltage fuse with a vehicle that will not b
s: Vehicle not ready to drive, propulsion warning
MIL or yellow warning lamp
Climate compressor or heater inoperative
c: Short circuit in a high-voltage auxiliary component (e.g. compressor, heater)
Fuse opened after overload or ageing
Faulty voltage measurement or software misdetection in the battery control module

P0A96.d: Some packs use two cooling fans; P0A96 reports an open or general fault in the control circuit of the second one. Ford documents it code-exact: on 2005–12 Escape Hybrid and 2006–11 Mariner Hybrid the traction battery control module may store P0A96, often together with P0A81 for fan 1, and the repair is to replace both high-voltage battery fans with a kit (about 3 hours, pack removal included).
s: Code found during other diagnosis, often no complaint
Check engine or hybrid warning
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions
c: Fan 2 motor or electronics failed (Ford replaces both fans)
Loose connector or broken wire to fan 2

P0A97.d: P0A97 is the fan 2 counterpart of P0A82: the second battery cooling fan is electrically reachable but does not reach its requested speed or does not turn at all. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Weak airflow from the battery vents
Reduced electric assist in warm weather
c: Dust or debris on fan 2 or in its duct
Blocked air intake to the battery

P0A98.d: P0A98 reports that battery cooling fan 2 keeps running after the controller has commanded it off; it mirrors P0A83 for fan 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Battery fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
12 V battery discharged after parking
Hybrid or check engine warning
c: Fan 2 control wire shorted to supply
Fan 2 internal controller ignores off command

P0A99.d: P0A99 reports a short to ground on the control circuit of the second battery cooling fan. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; Ford's two-fan Escape/Mariner Hybrid packs show that a second fan exists (there with P0A96).
s: Check engine or hybrid warning
Fan 2 does not run when commanded
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions
c: Fan 2 control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in fan 2 control input
Moisture or corrosion in the fan 2 connector

P0A9A.d: P0A9A reports a short to voltage on the control circuit of the second battery cooling fan. No manufacturer publishes this exact code; CARB requires the electronic outputs of battery thermal management to be checked for circuit faults.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning
Fan 2 runs constantly or not at all
Possible 12 V battery drain when parked
c: Fan 2 control wire shorted to supply voltage
Fan 2 control input internally open or shorted to supply
Corroded connector with leakage to supply

P0A9B.d: Temperature sensor A is one of the thermistors the battery controller uses to track cell or module temperature for cooling, charge limits and power limits. P0A9B is the general circuit code for this sensor: the controller finds an electrical fault it does not classify further as low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric assist, regeneration or charging power
Battery cooling fan or pump runs more than usual
c: Open, corroded or loose sensor wiring or connector inside the pack
Failed thermistor on the module or cell sensing board
Battery controller input or software fault

P0A9C.d: This is a plausibility check: the reading of temperature sensor A is compared with the other sensors in the same pack, which should agree within a few degrees. GM sets P0A9C (Type B, two trips) when sensor A deviates from the average of the others by more than 25 °C for 50 of 67 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids use more than 15 °C against each other sensor for 90 of 100 samples, other programs more than 20 °C.
s: Check engine light after two drive cycles
Reduced hybrid assist or charging power
Message such as battery too cold, plug in to warm (GM Volt)
c: Thermistor drifted or poorly seated on its cell or module
High-resistance connection in the sensor circuit shifting the reading
Battery controller calibration causing false sets (GM Volt update)
Genuine local temperature difference from a cooling or cell problem

P0A9D.d: Sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, so the voltage falls as the temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an absurdly hot cell. GM sets P0A9D (Type B, two trips) when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids use above 95 °C while the other sensors read below 70 °C, other programs above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Strongly reduced electric power or no EV mode
Battery cooling running at high speed without reason
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground or chafed inside the pack
Internally shorted thermistor on the sensing board
Moisture or coolant in the sensor connector
Battery controller software causing false sets (GM Volt)

P0A9E.d: With the NTC thermistor of sensor A on a pull-up circuit, an open sensor or wire drives the input voltage toward the reference, which the controller reads as an extremely cold cell. GM sets P0A9E (Type B, two trips) when the value falls below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids flag readings below -45 °C, other programs below -40 °C for 1.4 s.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message although it is not cold
Little or no electric drive and weak regeneration
c: Open sensor wire or unplugged connector inside the pack
Open (failed) thermistor on the sensing board
Signal shorted to the reference voltage
Battery controller software causing false sets (GM Volt)

P0A9F.d: Cell temperature changes slowly, so a reading that jumps back and forth points to the circuit, not the battery. GM monitors this by summing the absolute sample-to-sample change of sensor A over a 10-sample window every 100 ms; if the sum exceeds 10, that window fails, and four failed windows out of five set P0A9F as Type B (two trips) in the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02).
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Temporarily reduced hybrid or EV power
Battery temperature value jumps in the scan tool data
c: Loose, fretted or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Partly broken sensor wire that opens with vibration or heat
Electrical interference on the sensor line from high-voltage components

P0AA0.d: The positive main contactor is a high-voltage relay that connects the positive pole of the traction battery to the propulsion bus. P0AA0 is the general fault code for this contactor circuit, used when the controller sees a problem it does not split into stuck closed (P0AA1), stuck open (P0AA2) or the control-circuit codes P0AD9 to P0ADC.
s: Vehicle does not enter ready or propulsion-active mode
Hybrid or EV system warning with check engine light
Possible loss of propulsion while driving
c: Positive contactor or battery junction box worn or damaged
Fault in the contactor coil feed or its connector
Weak 12 V supply so the contactor does not pull in reliably

P0AA1.d: P0AA1 means the positive main contactor conducts although it should be open, typically because its contacts have welded. GM checks this with all contactors commanded open for over 120 s (or the bus already below 9 % of pack voltage): more than 30 V on the positive bus in 4 of 6 samples sets Type B (two trips, 19OBDG02).
s: Vehicle will not switch into ready or propulsion-active mode
Check engine light and service high voltage system message
Often stored together with P0AA4 or a slow discharge code such as P0C76
c: Positive contactor contacts welded, e.g. after high current or arcing
Battery or hybrid controller software (GM Volt 2019, Jeep 4xe updates)
Faulty battery disconnect unit (GM Bolt EV bulletin)
Bus voltage sensing error making an open contactor look closed

P0AA2.d: P0AA2 means the positive main contactor does not close, or does not conduct, when the controller commands it closed, so the high-voltage bus cannot be energised from the pack. Audi documents it for the 2020-2022 Q5 e quattro and 2021-2022 A7 e quattro plug-in hybrids: the car does not start and the battery management module stores P0AA2 (often with P0AA5).
s: Vehicle does not start or reach ready mode
Service high voltage battery or hybrid warning message
Possible sudden loss of propulsion if the contactor opens while driving
c: Oxidised contact surfaces after long standing or high humidity (Audi)
Failed battery junction box or burnt contactor
Contactor coil not energised due to wiring or 12 V supply fault

P0AA3.d: The negative main contactor switches the negative pole of the traction battery onto the propulsion bus; together with the positive contactor it isolates the pack completely when the car is off. P0AA3 is the general code for this contactor circuit when the fault is not reported more precisely as stuck closed (P0AA4), stuck open (P0AA5) or a control-circuit fault (P0ADD to P0AE0).
s: Vehicle does not enter ready mode
Hybrid or EV system warning with check engine light
Charging may be refused
c: Negative contactor or battery junction box worn or damaged
Fault in the contactor coil wiring or connector
Battery controller driver or software fault

P0AA4.d: P0AA4 reports that the negative main contactor still conducts while it should be open, usually through welded contacts, so the pack is no longer fully isolated on the negative side. GM tests it once all contactors have been commanded open for more than 120 s, or the bus has already decayed below 9 % of pack voltage: over 30 V on the negative bus in 4 of 6 samples at 12.5 ms sets Type B (two trips, 19OBDG02).
s: Vehicle will not start or switch into ready mode
Check engine light and high voltage system message
Often stored together with P0AA1 or the slow discharge code P0C76
c: Negative contactor contacts welded after high current or arcing
Battery or hybrid controller software (GM Volt 2019, Jeep 4xe updates)
Faulty battery disconnect unit (GM Bolt EV bulletin)

P0AA5.d: P0AA5 is set when the negative main contactor stays open or fails to conduct after the controller has commanded it closed, so the negative side of the high-voltage bus never connects. Audi reports it, alone or with P0AA2, on the 2020-2022 Q5 e quattro and 2021-2022 A7 e quattro plug-in hybrids with a no-start complaint; the stated cause is oxidation of the contact surfaces in the battery junction box after very long
s: Vehicle does not start or reach ready mode
Hybrid or high voltage battery warning
Charging not possible
c: Oxidised contact surfaces after long standing or high humidity (Audi)
Failed battery junction box or burnt negative contactor
Contactor coil not energised due to wiring or 12 V supply fault

P0AA6.d: The high-voltage system floats free of the chassis, and an isolation monitor measures the resistance from each HV rail to body ground. P0AA6 sets when that resistance falls below a calibrated limit.
s: Check engine and hybrid or EV system warning lights
Vehicle will not charge or will not enter ready mode after restart
Stop safely now message or reduced power
c: Coolant or moisture inside the battery pack, inverter or drive motor
Chafed or crushed orange HV cable shorting to the body
Insulation breakdown in the electric A/C compressor or a motor winding
Electrolyte leakage or contamination inside the battery sections

P0AA7.d: To measure isolation, the battery controller reads the voltage of each HV rail against chassis ground through an isolation sensor circuit and can switch in a known bias resistor. P0AA7 means this measuring circuit itself does not work, so the controller can no longer judge isolation.
s: Check engine and EV system service warnings
Power reduced or speed limited until the system is switched off and on
Regenerative braking warning on some models
c: Failed isolation bias switch or measuring circuit inside the battery controller
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)
Open or loose isolation sense lead or connector at the battery

P0AA8.d: The two isolation sensor readings, positive rail to ground and negative rail to ground, should together equal the total pack voltage. P0AA8 is the plausibility check of that relation.
s: Check engine and hybrid or EV system warnings
Reduced power or speed limit until restart
Isolation monitoring unavailable, so related faults may go unreported
c: Isolation measuring amplifier or reference in the battery controller out of tolerance
Pack voltage sense lead fault making the comparison value wrong
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)

P0AA9.d: P0AA9 reports that the isolation sensor signal sits below its valid window, typically because the sense line or the measuring input is pulled toward ground or has lost its supply. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables flag it when the sensor reads under 5 V with the bias switch open in 320 of 400 samples (about 5 s), Type B, two trips; the 2013 GM table uses a negative mid-pack reading under 5 V with contactors closed.
s: Check engine and EV system warning lights
Reduced power or speed limit on some models
c: Isolation sense line shorted to ground or open input
Failed isolation measuring circuit in the battery controller
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)

P0AAA.d: P0AAA is the high-side counterpart of P0AA9: the isolation sensor reports a rail-to-ground voltage above anything the pack can produce. GM's tables tie the limit to the pack: over 333 V in the 2016 table and over 416 V in the 2019 table, each in 320 of 400 samples with the bias switch open, Type B, two trips.
s: Check engine and hybrid or EV warning lights
Isolation monitoring disabled while the code is active
c: Open ground or reference in the isolation measuring circuit
Failed isolation input stage in the battery controller
Sense lead shorted to another HV potential inside the pack

P0AAB.d: P0AAB covers an isolation sensor signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's hybrid tables use only P0AA7 to P0AAA for the measuring circuit.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lights that come and go
Occasional power limitation that clears after restart
c: Electrical noise misinterpreted by controller software
Loose or corroded sense connector at the battery controller
Failing isolation measuring circuit inside the controller

P0AAC.d: Air-cooled hybrid batteries carry a thermistor in the cooling air path; GM calls sensor A the inlet air sensor. The battery controller uses it to run the fan and to judge cooling.
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Battery cooling fan runs constantly or at fixed speed
Reduced electric assist in hot conditions
c: Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connector or wiring at the air duct
Battery controller input or reference voltage fault

P0AAD.d: P0AAD is the plausibility check for battery air temperature sensor A: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit other temperatures. GM documents two methods.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery cooling fan behaves unusually
c: Thermistor drifted or stuck at a plausible value
Sensor displaced from the air stream or duct blocked
Fault in the comparison sensor (outlet air or cell temperature)

P0AAE.d: The battery air temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor, so a low signal voltage reads as very hot air. P0AAE sets when the signal stays below the lower limit, usually a short to ground.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery cooling fan runs at high speed without reason
Reduced electric assist and regeneration
c: Sensor signal wire chafed and shorted to ground

P0AAF.d: Air temperature sensor A is the thermistor GM places at the cooling air inlet of air-cooled hybrid packs. Being an NTC type, a high signal voltage means the controller sees implausibly cold air, typically from an open wire or a lost ground.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Scan tool shows inlet air near -40 °C regardless of weather
Battery fan runs on a fixed default speed
c: Open signal or ground wire between sensor and battery controller
Connector at the air inlet duct loose or with pushed-back pin

P0AB0.d: P0AB0 flags a battery air temperature sensor A signal that jumps faster than real air temperature can change, usually a sign of a loose contact rather than a dead sensor. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's two-mode and 2013 tables for sensor A only list the low, high and plausibility codes.
s: Hybrid warning light that comes and goes
Inlet air reading jumps in live data
Battery fan speed changes without obvious reason
c: Loose or corroded contact at the inlet air sensor connector
Wire chafed through at the duct, intermittently touching ground
Electrical interference on the sensor line

P0AB1.d: Air temperature sensor B is a second thermistor in the battery cooling air path; in GM's two-mode hybrid tables it is the outlet air sensor behind the modules. P0AB1 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller sees an electrical fault without sorting it into low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid or check engine warning light
Battery fan runs on a default setting
Possibly reduced electric assist
c: Damaged wiring or poor contact at the outlet air sensor

P0AB2.d: P0AB2 checks whether air temperature sensor B reads sensibly. GM uses it on the full-size two-mode hybrids, where sensor B measures outlet air: in the 2011 and 2013 tables, with the battery fan commanded on, the outlet air may not be more than 10 °C warmer than the hottest battery module, 90 of 100 samples, Type B, two trips.
s: Hybrid or check engine warning light
Outlet air reads clearly above module temperatures in live data
Usually no change in driving behavior
c: Outlet air thermistor drifted from its characteristic
Sensor displaced from its position in the air duct
Battery module temperature sensor used for comparison reads wrong

P0AB3.d: P0AB3 means the signal of air temperature sensor B sits below its valid range. Because the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage translates into very hot air, so a short to ground is the usual cause.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery fan runs loud even when the pack is cool
Reduced electric assist and regeneration
c: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or debris bridging the connector pins

P0AB4.d: P0AB4 reports a signal from air temperature sensor B above the valid range. For an NTC thermistor that reads as extremely cold air, which points to an open circuit, a broken ground or a disconnected plug.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Outlet air shows about -40 °C in live data
Battery fan on default operation
c: Open signal or ground wire of sensor B
Connector not refitted after battery or duct work

P0AB5.d: P0AB5 is set when the signal of battery air temperature sensor B fluctuates in a way real air temperature cannot, typically from an intermittent contact. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's two-mode tables, which use sensor B as the outlet air sensor, list only P0AB2 to P0AB4.
s: Hybrid warning light that appears intermittently
Outlet air value jumps in live data
No noticeable driving change in most cases
c: Loose or corroded terminal at sensor B
Partly broken wire near the outlet duct
Interference coupled into the sensor line

P0AB6.d: Some engines sit on switchable or actively driven hydraulic mounts whose solenoid or actuator is energised by the engine controller. P0AB6 reports that the driver output for the second mount (B) sees an open or otherwise faulty circuit.
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable vibration at idle or with cylinder deactivation active
Cylinder deactivation may be suspended on some models
c: Broken or chafed control wire to the mount actuator
Corroded or loose connector at the mount (splash zone)
Mount solenoid or actuator coil open internally
Output driver in the engine controller defective

P0AB7.d: P0AB7 means the engine controller sees the control line of active engine mount B pulled too low, the usual signature of a short to ground or an actuator coil with too little resistance. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary lists it among the active-mount checks for bank 2: the output driver flags the fault continuously and the PCM matures it within roughly 5 seconds.
s: Check engine light on
Increased vibration felt through seat and steering wheel at idle
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water ingress in the mount connector

P0AB8.d: With P0AB8 the controller finds the control circuit of active engine mount B at too high a level, for example because the line has a short to battery voltage or the driver cannot pull it down. Ford names the code in its 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary as the bank 2 high fault of the active-mount circuit check, which runs continuously and needs about 5 seconds of driver-reported fault before a code is stored.
s: Check engine light on
Rougher feel at idle and when pulling away
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Output driver in the engine controller defective

P0AB9.d: Despite the broad title, GM uses P0AB9 for one concrete check: a failed engine auto-start or auto-stop in its hybrids, including an engine stall during that process. In the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the hybrid controller sets the code when the engine still reports no torque about 15 seconds into an auto-start although more than 20 Nm is commanded, provided fuel level is sufficient and no cam or crank fault is prese
s: Check engine light on
Engine hesitates, fails or stalls when restarting at a stop
Auto-stop disabled for the rest of the trip
c: Fuel delivery problem (weak pump, nearly empty tank, clogged filter)
Ignition or injector fault that prevents the engine from firing
Starter-generator or motor unable to spin the engine to start speed

P0ABA.d: The battery management system measures the total voltage of the high-voltage pack through a dedicated sense circuit and uses it for state of charge, power limits and contactor checks. P0ABA is the general circuit fault for sense circuit A, set when the reading is unusable without being clearly low, high or erratic.
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Reduced electric assist or EV range
Vehicle may not enter ready mode
c: Damaged or loose voltage sense lead inside the battery pack
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
Blown sense fuse or failed divider resistor

P0ABB.d: P0ABB is a plausibility check: the measured pack voltage is within electrical limits but does not agree with what the individual cells add up to. GM documents it in several hybrid tables.
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Erratic state-of-charge display
Reduced electric power
c: Pack voltage measurement drifted (divider or input aging)
Faulty cell voltage tap distorting the cell sum

P0ABC.d: P0ABC is stored when the pack voltage sensor reports a value below anything the battery could really have, pointing to a short to ground or a lost sense signal rather than a discharged pack. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set it below 4.8 V with system voltage above 10.2 V, after 8 failed samples out of 10 taken every 25 ms, and rate it Type A with MIL on the first trip.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode
Engine runs continuously, no electric drive
c: Sense line shorted to ground or disconnected
Sense fuse or link open so no voltage reaches the input

P0ABD.d: The counterpart to P0ABC: the pack voltage reading is above the highest value the battery could physically reach, which suggests an open reference, a failed divider or a damaged input rather than real overcharging. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set P0ABD above 392 V, again with 8 failed samples out of 10 at 25 ms intervals and Type A, so the MIL comes on immediately.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Electric drive limited or unavailable
c: Open ground or reference side of the sense circuit
Voltage divider component failed in the battery controller

P0ABE.d: P0ABE flags a pack voltage signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of changing smoothly, as a battery voltage physically would. A loose sense connection or a cracked solder joint inside the pack are the classic triggers.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Sudden short drops in electric power
c: Loose or fretted voltage sense connection
Cracked solder or crimp joint on the sense board
Electrical noise from damaged shielding or ground

P0ABF.d: The pack current sensor, usually a Hall-effect unit around the main cable, tells the battery controller how much current flows in and out. P0ABF is the general fault of sensor A.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Reduced electric power and erratic charge display
Vehicle may not go ready
c: Sensor supply, ground or signal wire faulty
Sensor not seated around the conductor after repair

P0AC0.d: P0AC0 belongs to the battery current sensor family, not to battery cooling. It reports a sensor whose reading is electrically valid but implausible.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
State of charge display drifts or jumps
Reduced electric assist
c: Unstable sensor supply or reference voltage

P0AC1.d: P0AC1 is set when the output of the pack current sensor falls below the valid window, so that the converted current would be an impossible discharge or charge value. GM documents it in several hybrid tables.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Electric drive limited or vehicle will not go ready
c: Sensor 5 V supply open or shorted

P0AC2.d: With P0AC2 the current sensor output sits above its valid window, which after conversion would mean an implausibly large current in the opposite direction to P0AC1. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set it when the Hall-effect sensor reads above 274.6 A in 8 of 10 samples taken every 25 ms, again as Type A with immediate MIL.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Battery power limited, engine runs more often
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V supply or another voltage

P0AC3.d: P0AC3 describes a battery current signal that jumps, spikes or drops out in a way real current flow could not explain, typically through a loose connector, a chafed signal wire or interference on the sensor ground. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Short drops in electric power while driving
c: Loose or corroded current sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact
Interference on sensor ground or shield

P0AC4.d: In many hybrids the hybrid powertrain controller has its own emission-related diagnostics but does not drive the malfunction indicator lamp itself. When it detects such a fault it sends a MIL request to the engine controller, which then stores P0AC4 as a pointer.
s: Check engine light on (caused by the underlying hybrid fault)
Further codes present only in the hybrid controller
c: Emission-related fault stored in the hybrid controller
Request still present because codes were cleared only in the engine controller

P0AC5.d: Battery temperature sensor B is one of several thermistors that measure cell or module temperature inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin calls it sensor 2 of nine. P0AC5 is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Charging may be slower on plug-in models
c: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor B and sensing board
Fault in the battery controller input stage

P0AC6.d: P0AC6 is the plausibility test for battery temperature sensor B: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. GM documents several calibrations.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
One sensor reading far off the others in live data
Battery too cold message on the Volt in mild weather
c: Controller software flags the sensor falsely (GM Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Sensor B drifted from its characteristic
Corroded contact adding resistance in the sensor circuit
Real temperature difference from a weak cell or blocked cooling

P0AC7.d: P0AC7 means the voltage of battery temperature sensor B is below its valid range. GM's sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low voltage equals an extremely hot reading, usually from a short to ground.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor B shows an implausibly high temperature
Charging and drive power reduced
c: Sensor B signal shorted to ground inside the pack harness
Controller software setting the code falsely (Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture or coolant at the sensing board connector

P0AC8.d: P0AC8 reports that battery temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range, which for an NTC thermistor reads as extreme cold. An open wire, a disconnected sensing board plug or a broken sensor are typical.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message although it is not cold
Strongly reduced charging and electric power
c: Open signal or return wire of sensor B
Controller software issue on the Volt (bulletin 18-NA-342)
Signal shorted to the reference voltage

P0AC9.d: P0AC9 catches a battery temperature sensor B signal that changes erratically. Pack temperatures move slowly because of the large thermal mass, so rapid swings point to a bad connection.
s: Hybrid warning light that comes and goes
Sensor B value jumps in live data
Occasional power limitation
c: Loose terminal or unlatched connector at the sensing board
Partly broken sensor wire inside the pack
Interference from high-voltage switching on the sensor line

P0ACA.d: Battery temperature sensor C is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack, corresponding to sensor 3 in GM's Volt bulletin. P0ACA covers a general electrical fault in its circuit that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Further battery sensor codes may be stored
c: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor C and sensing board
Fault in the battery controller input stage

P0ACB.d: With P0ACB the controller judges battery temperature sensor C implausible: its value deviates too far from what the other pack sensors report. GM applies the same limits as for sensors A and B.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor C reads clearly off the others after a long soak
Possibly reduced charge and drive power
c: Sensor C drifted from its characteristic
Controller software flags the sensor falsely (GM Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Real temperature difference in the module monitored by sensor C

P0ACC.d: P0ACC sets when the signal of battery temperature sensor C drops below the valid voltage window. For the NTC sensors GM uses, that equals an impossibly hot reading, most often caused by a short to ground in the pack wiring.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor C shows an implausibly high temperature
Reduced charging and electric drive power
c: Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Controller software setting the code falsely (Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture at the sensing board connector

P0ACD.d: P0ACD indicates that battery temperature sensor C reports a voltage above its plausible range, which an NTC sensor translates into extreme cold. Common reasons are an open circuit, a pin backed out of the sensing board connector or a cracked thermistor.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message in mild weather
Strongly reduced charging and electric power
c: Open signal or return wire of sensor C
Controller software issue on the Volt (bulletin 18-NA-342)

P0ACE.d: P0ACE flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor C, meaning the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips.
s: Hybrid warning light that appears intermittently
Sensor C value jumps in live data
Occasional power limitation
c: Loose terminal or unlatched connector at sensor C
Partly broken sensor wire inside the pack
Fault on the battery sensing board affecting several inputs

P0ACF.d: Air-cooled traction batteries can use several blowers; P0ACF belongs to the third one and means the battery controller sees an open or otherwise invalid control line while it drives fan 3. CARB 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3)(B) requires the electrical inputs and outputs of the battery thermal management to be monitored like other comprehensive components.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light, often with check engine light
Electric drive power reduced when the battery gets warm
No fan noise from the battery area when cooling is expected
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at fan 3
Broken control wire between battery controller and fan 3
Fan motor or its built-in driver open internally
Fan output stage in the battery controller defective

P0AD0.d: P0AD0 is a functional fault: the control line of battery fan 3 may be electrically fine, but the blower does not deliver what was commanded, or stays still. Depending on design, the controller compares fan speed feedback with the request, or, as a Honda patent describes, compares the expected battery temperature change for the known cooling capacity with the measured one.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light
Power or regeneration limited after longer drives or in heat
Battery temperature rises faster than usual
c: Fan intake or duct blocked by dirt, pet hair or objects (often under or beside a seat)
Worn bearings or debris slowing the fan wheel
Speed feedback signal from fan 3 missing or implausible
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the fan

P0AD1.d: P0AD1 is the counterpart to P0AD0: fan 3 of the traction battery keeps turning although the controller has switched it off or commanded a lower level. A speed feedback or the current in the fan circuit shows that the blower still runs.
s: Battery fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
12 V battery discharged after standing
Hybrid or EV warning light
c: Fan output stage in battery controller or fan module stuck on
Control wire chafed against a supply voltage

P0AD2.d: P0AD2 reports that the control signal for battery fan 3 is pulled too low, typically a short to ground on the line between battery controller and blower. Such fans are mostly speed-controlled by a PWM duty cycle, as a Toyota patent on battery fan control explains.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light, often with check engine light
Electric drive power reduced when the battery gets warm
No fan noise from the battery area when cooling is expected
c: Control wire chafed through to body ground
Internal short in fan 3 motor or its electronics
Moisture or spilled liquid in the fan connector
Output stage in the battery controller defective

P0AD3.d: With P0AD3 the battery controller finds the control line of cooling fan 3 at a voltage that is too high for the commanded state, pointing to a short to a supply voltage or a fan input that no longer pulls the line down. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM's analogous fan 1 code P0A85 trips when the control voltage exceeds 9 V while the fan is driven, Type B.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light
Fan 3 runs constantly or not at all
Reduced electric power when the battery is warm
c: Control wire shorted to 12 V or another supply
Fan electronics no longer loading the control line
Bent or bridged pins in the fan connector

P0AD4.d: P0AD4 is a system-level check of air-cooled traction batteries: the controller concludes that too little air passes the cells, for example because the cell temperatures rise faster than the commanded fan level allows, as a Honda fan diagnosis patent describes. CARB 1968.2 asks for a functional check of the battery cooling performance where feasible.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Reduced electric assist or start-stop not available
Battery fan runs loud for long periods
c: Cabin air intake grille or duct of the battery blocked (bags, clothing, dust, pet hair)
Battery air filter clogged, where fitted
Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Ram eTorque, fixed by update)

P0AD5.d: Some air-cooled battery packs route their cooling air through a motorized flap that switches between cabin air, recirculation or an outlet. P0AD5 means the battery controller finds the drive circuit of this valve A open or otherwise faulty.
s: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual
c: Loose or corroded connector at the flap actuator
Broken wire in the actuator harness
Output stage in battery controller defective

P0AD6.d: P0AD6 flags that the air flow valve A of the battery cooling does not behave as expected: the circuit is intact, but position, travel or the learned end stops do not fit the command. Audi documents exactly this code as P0AD600 on the 2012-15 Q5 hybrid (TSB 2038152): a software error made the battery management module J841 lose the learned end stops of the air supply valve, electric and hybrid drive were disabled, and
s: Hybrid drive system error message in the cluster
Electric and hybrid operation no longer available
Check engine light on
c: Battery controller software loses learned end stops (Audi Q5 hybrid, fixed by update)
Flap binding from dirt or a deformed duct
Actuator gears or position feedback worn
End stops not relearned after battery or actuator work

P0AD7.d: P0AD7 sets when the control circuit of the battery air flow valve A reads too low a voltage, usually a short to ground in the line or actuator. The valve is a motorized flap in the battery cooling duct, as in the Audi Q5 hybrid cooling module, whose bulletin covers the range/performance sibling P0AD6.
s: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual
c: Actuator control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the flap actuator

P0AD8.d: With P0AD8 the battery controller sees too high a voltage in the drive circuit of air flow valve A, typically a short to a supply voltage or an actuator that no longer draws current. The component is the motorized flap that directs cooling air through an air-cooled traction battery, documented for example in Audi's Q5 hybrid bulletin on the related code P0AD6.
s: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Actuator no longer loading the circuit
Bridged or bent pins in the connector

P0AD9.d: The positive main contactor connects the traction battery to the high-voltage bus; its coil is driven by the battery or hybrid controller. P0AD9 covers an open in this coil circuit.
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible
c: Open in the contactor coil or its pigtail inside the battery disconnect unit
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the battery disconnect unit
Broken control wire in the battery harness
High-side driver in the battery controller defective

P0ADA.d: P0ADA describes a positive contactor coil circuit that is electrically present but does not behave plausibly: coil current, voltage or response time outside the expected window, for instance due to high resistance or an unstable PWM hold signal. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM, which details the positive contactor driver codes P0AD9, P0ADB and P0ADC with Type B logic and sample counters, does not lis
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible
c: High resistance in coil wiring or connector (corrosion, fretting)
Contactor coil degraded or partially shorted
Low 12 V supply during contactor closing

P0ADB.d: P0ADB means the drive circuit of the positive main contactor reads too low, mostly a short to ground. GM uses it widely: 2016-19 tables set it when the control voltage stays under 5.35 V with the contactor commanded on, 13 of 16 samples, Type B.
s: Vehicle does not start; multiple warnings in the cluster
Hybrid or EV warning light
Charging not possible
c: Coil control wire shorted to ground
Battery controller software sets the code (Audi, Dodge bulletins)
Driver stage in the battery controller defective

P0ADC.d: P0ADC indicates that the positive contactor drive circuit carries too much voltage for the commanded state, usually a short to battery voltage. In GM's 2016-19 hybrid tables the driver output, with the contactor commanded off, reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V for 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B with two trips.
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready
Possible related stuck-closed codes
c: Coil control wire shorted to 12 V
Damaged harness or connector at the battery disconnect unit
Driver stage in the battery controller shorted

P0ADD.d: The negative main contactor closes the return path of the traction battery; P0ADD reports an open in its coil drive circuit. GM documents the code in parallel to the positive side: tables since model year 2011 detect open load in the HPC2 and store it after two trips; 2016-19 tables evaluate a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V while off, 40 of 50 samples, Type B, and 2019 tables add a coil current check below 1
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible
c: Open in negative contactor coil or its pigtail
Loose or corroded connector at the battery disconnect unit
Broken control wire in the battery harness
Driver in the battery controller defective

P0ADE.d: P0ADE is set when the coil circuit of the negative main contactor works electrically but its values are implausible, such as coil current or hold voltage out of range or a slow response after the command. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM, whose tables cover the negative contactor driver codes P0ADD, P0ADF and P0AE0 in detail, does not use P0ADE.
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible
c: High resistance in coil wiring or connector

P0ADF.d: P0ADF reports that the drive circuit of the negative main contactor is pulled too low, typically a short to ground in the coil line. GM documents the code in its 2016-19 hybrid tables: control voltage below 5.35 V while the contactor is commanded on, 13 of 16 samples at 12.5 ms (20 of 25 in one 2016 group), Type B with two trips, enabled above about 9 to 10 V on the 12 V system.
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible
c: Coil control wire shorted to ground
Moisture in the battery disconnect unit connector
Driver in the battery controller defective

P0AE0.d: P0AE0 is stored when the negative contactor drive circuit shows too high a voltage for its state, which mostly means a short to battery voltage. GM's 2016-19 hybrid tables set it with the contactor commanded off and the driver output between 5.27 and 19.7 V for 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips.
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready
Possible additional stuck-closed code
c: Coil control wire shorted to 12 V
Damaged harness or connector at the battery disconnect unit
Driver stage in the battery controller shorted

P0AE1.d: Before the main contactors close, a precharge contactor routes battery current through a resistor so the inverter capacitors fill slowly instead of drawing a damaging inrush. P0AE1 is the general fault of this precharge path when it is not split into stuck closed (P0AE2), stuck open (P0AE3) or a driver fault (P0AE4 to P0AE7).
s: Hybrid or EV system warning in the cluster
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
Charging not possible
c: Defective solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda IMA)
Precharge contactor or precharge resistor failed
Fault logged by battery controller software after an interrupted charging sequence
Wiring or connector fault in the contactor circuit

P0AE2.d: P0AE2 means the precharge path conducts although it should be open, for example welded contacts or a precharge switch that no longer turns off. GM's 2011 Volt table checks it once per precharge event: if the bus voltage already exceeds 80 % of pack voltage before precharge begins, the precharge FET is judged stuck closed, 4 of 4 samples, Type A with MIL after one trip.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Wrench symbol or service message in the cluster
c: Precharge contactor contacts welded or precharge switch shorted
Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Audi, Stellantis bulletins)
Contactor driver held on by a short to power
Bus voltage not discharged before the next precharge

P0AE3.d: P0AE3 is set when the precharge path does not conduct after it has been commanded closed, so the bus voltage fails to rise and the main contactors are not allowed to close. GM documents several cases: preliminary information PIC6165A for the 2016-17 Chevrolet Volt describes a rare P0AE3 in cool weather right after a completed charge, without driveability effects; parts should not be replaced, a new calibration follow
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL or service engine soon light on
No battery charge level shown after switching on
c: Battery controller calibration sets the code under certain conditions (GM Volt, Audi)
Precharge contactor contacts burnt or coil not pulling in
Precharge resistor or its fuse open
Internal fault in the battery disconnect unit

P0AE4.d: P0AE4 concerns the circuit that drives the coil of precharge contactor A, not its contacts. GM uses it in many hybrid and EV tables, with changing logic: the 2016 and 2019 OBDG02 tables look for an open high-side driver circuit, a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V while commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Charging not possible
c: Open control wire or loose connector at the contactor coil
Control wire shorted to 12 V (GM 2011 and 2019 logic)
Driver stage in the battery or hybrid controller defective

P0AE5.d: P0AE5 reports that the precharge function works electrically but does not deliver the expected result, so the controller judges the circuit implausible. Ford documents it in special service message SSM 47129: 2013-18 C-MAX and Fusion Hybrid and Energi models and the MKZ Hybrid may not start, with P0AE5 stored in the battery energy control module.
s: Vehicle does not start or become ready
Red warning triangle or hybrid warning in the cluster
Possible additional codes from the faulty high-voltage consumer
c: High-voltage consumer with low internal resistance (DC/DC converter, coolant heater, A/C compressor)
Precharge resistor degraded or wrong value
Precharge contactor responding slowly or with high contact resistance

P0AE6.d: P0AE6 means the control line of precharge contactor A is pulled too low, usually a short to ground. GM documents it in several programs.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid warning on
Engine start or electric drive unavailable
c: Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Open circuit on low-side driven designs (GM eAssist)
Driver stage in the battery controller defective

P0AE7.d: P0AE7 is stored when the control line of precharge contactor A carries too much voltage for its commanded state, typically a short to the 12 V supply. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the high-side driver output reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V while the contactor is commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips.
s: Vehicle may not start or become ready
MIL and hybrid warning on
Possible additional stuck-closed code P0AE2
c: Control wire shorted to 12 V supply
Driver stage stuck on in the battery controller

P0AE8.d: Battery temperature sensor D is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the matching codes as temperature sensor 4 of nine. P0AE8 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller finds an electrical fault without classifying it as low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Further battery sensor codes may be stored
c: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor D and sensing board
Fault in the battery controller input stage

P0AE9.d: P0AE9 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor D, GM's sensor 4: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables it fails when the value is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the eAssist table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after a long module off time; GM's 2
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Battery Too Cold message despite mild weather (Volt)
Reduced charge and electric drive power
c: Temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance
Genuine local temperature difference in one battery module
Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit

P0AEA.d: P0AEA means the voltage of battery temperature sensor D is below its valid range. GM uses NTC thermistors with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an extremely hot cell, usually from a short to ground.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Charge and drive power strongly limited
Battery cooling running more than usual
c: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or damage on the battery sensing board

P0AEB.d: P0AEB reports that battery temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensors this reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Battery Too Cold message (Volt)
Charging and electric drive restricted
c: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor D

P0AEC.d: P0AEC flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor D: the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips, may go out again
Jumping battery temperature in live data
Occasional power limitation
c: Loose terminal or connector not fully latched at sensor D
Partly broken or chafed sensor wire
Fault on the battery sensing board

P0AED.d: The inverter of an electric drive motor carries thermistors near its power switches so the controller can derate before the IGBTs overheat. In GM's hybrid tables, inverter temperature sensor A is the phase U sensor of the inverter for motor A.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive power
Possible loss of electric drive
c: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor

P0AEE.d: P0AEE checks whether inverter temperature sensor A reads sensibly. GM's 2016 to 2019 tables compare it after a cold soak with an average temperature of the vehicle; more than 20 °C apart sets Type B, two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, often without drivability change
Drive system fault warning (Audi)
Vehicle may not start in hybrid mode
c: Controller software error (Audi Q5/A7 e quattro bulletin)
Inverter temperature sensor A drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module (e.g. Honda MPI solder joints)

P0AEF.d: P0AEF means the signal of inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. GM describes it as an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an impossibly hot inverter, usually a short to ground or an internal sensor fault.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Electric drive power cut back strongly
Vehicle may not start (Jeep Compass PHEV)
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing

P0AF0.d: P0AF0 reports a signal from inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range, which for an NTC sensor reads as an extremely cold inverter: open wire, lost ground or a broken sensor. GM's 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a really cold car does not trigger it; Type B, two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Reduced electric drive power
Traction motor noise or inoperative A/C (Kia)
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Motor control unit software (Kia Sorento Hybrid 2025)
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter

P0AF1.d: P0AF1 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of failing permanently. Inverter heat sinks are liquid-cooled and change temperature smoothly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or an internal fault in the sensing circuit.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief power reductions while driving
Jumping inverter temperature in live data
c: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal

P0AF2.d: Inverter temperature sensor B is, in GM's hybrid tables, the phase U thermistor of the second inverter, the one that drives motor B in two-motor systems. P0AF2 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive or generator power
Higher fuel consumption in hybrid operation
c: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor

P0AF3.d: P0AF3 is the plausibility test for inverter temperature sensor B, the phase U sensor of GM's motor B inverter. In the 2016 to 2019 tables the sensor is compared after a cold soak with a calculated average vehicle temperature; a difference above 20 °C sets the code, Type B, two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Often no noticeable drivability change
Further inverter temperature codes may be stored
c: Inverter temperature sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak

P0AF4.d: P0AF4 reports a signal of inverter temperature sensor B below the valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up, so a low voltage reads as an inverter far hotter than possible, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault in the motor B inverter.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Motor B power strongly limited
Reduced hybrid assist and regeneration
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing

P0AF5.d: P0AF5 means inverter temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Reduced motor B power
Implausibly cold inverter temperature in live data
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter

P0AF6.d: P0AF6 targets an inverter temperature sensor B signal that jumps or drops out briefly. Since the heat sink of the motor B inverter is liquid-cooled and warms or cools gradually, abrupt changes in the reading indicate a contact problem or an intermittent fault in the sensing circuit rather than real temperature.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief reductions of motor B power
Jumping inverter temperature in live data
c: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal

P0AF7.d: The 14 V power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery in hybrids and EVs. P0AF7 reports that its internal temperature has exceeded the protection limit, a real overheat rather than a sensor circuit fault.
s: Warning lamp or 12 V charging warning
Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights
Comfort consumers switched off
c: Restricted cooling, weak coolant pump or failed cooling fan
Sustained high 12 V load or weak 12 V battery
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter

P0AF8.d: P0AF8 compares the battery pack voltage reported by the battery controller with an independent measurement on the high-voltage bus. GM calls it system voltage correlation: with the contactors closed, the 2019 tables fail it when the pack reading differs from the inverter bus voltage by more than 13.95 V, or from the charger bus voltage by more than 14.95 V, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Battery saver or low battery message
Intermittent no crank or reduced hybrid power
c: Loose or arcing high-voltage battery cable connection
Pack or bus voltage sensing circuit inaccurate
Low 12 V supply or loose 12 V power fuse affecting the measuring modules
High resistance in a pack fuse or main contactor

P0AF9.d: P0AF9 is meant for a traction battery voltage that fluctuates more than load changes can explain, for example through a loose terminal, an intermittent contactor or a cell group that collapses under load. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, covers system voltage with P0AF8 (correlation), P0AFA and P0AFB (low and high), and reports uneven cell groups as P0BBE pack voltage variation, w
s: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning
Sudden power reductions while driving
Code may come and go without lasting symptoms
c: Loose high-voltage terminal or busbar connection
Degraded cell group collapsing under load

P0AFA.d: P0AFA protects the traction battery from deep discharge: the pack voltage, or in some versions any cell voltage, has fallen below a temperature-dependent limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it after 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack or 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch it so that only a technician command can clear it.
s: Vehicle does not start; restart blocked while the code is latched
Reduced or lost propulsion before the no-start
Plug-in charging not possible
c: Pack drained by repeated failed engine starts or long standing
Open high-voltage fuse or manual disconnect
Loose or high-resistance ground on 48 V systems

P0AFB.d: P0AFB guards against overcharging: the pack voltage, or a single cell, exceeds a temperature-dependent upper limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack and 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch the code until a technician clears it by command; the 2011 Volt table also uses Type A.
s: Hybrid system or MIL warning
Start-stop or regenerative braking disabled
Possible no crank on mild hybrids
c: Loose or arcing battery cable causing voltage spikes
Control unit software allows overvoltage (Mercedes 48 V bulletins)
Cell imbalance so that one cell overcharges
Faulty voltage sensing reporting too high a value

P0AFC.d: Some hybrid packs carry a separate sensor module that measures block voltages and passes them to the battery controller; Toyota calls it the battery voltage sensor or battery smart unit. P0AFC reports a fault of this module itself, such as a failed self-check or disturbed data transfer.
s: MIL and check hybrid system warning on
Hybrid drive disabled or reduced
Code may return when the radio transmitter is used
c: Radio interference from an aftermarket antenna near the battery (Toyota Camry Hybrid)
Battery voltage sensor module internally defective
Supply or communication wiring of the sensor module faulty

P0AFD.d: P0AFD indicates that the traction battery is colder than its permitted operating range. At very low temperatures cell resistance rises and charging risks lithium plating, so the controller restricts or blocks charging and discharging.
s: Battery too cold message in the cluster
Reduced electric power or electric drive unavailable
Charging slow or not possible until the pack warms up
c: Vehicle parked unplugged in extreme cold
Battery heater or coolant heater not working
Temperature sensor reading too cold (sensor or software)

P0AFE.d: Many hybrids raise the battery voltage with a step-up (boost) converter before it reaches the inverters; Toyota's second-generation Hybrid Synergy Drive, for example, boosts a pack of around 200 V to 500 V or more. The converter needs a minimum input voltage to reach its target without excessive current.
s: Hybrid system warning
Reduced acceleration and electric assist
Engine runs more often than usual
c: Pack deeply discharged or weak under load
High-resistance connection between battery and converter
Converter input voltage measured too low

P0AFF.d: A step-down (buck) DC/DC converter, often called the accessory power module, supplies the 12 V system from the high-voltage or 48 V bus. To regulate its output it needs an input voltage above a minimum.
s: Battery or charging system warning light
12 V battery discharges, electrical consumers fail
Hybrid or start-stop functions restricted
c: High-voltage or 48 V bus voltage too low (discharged pack, open contactor)
High-resistance input connection or fuse of the DC/DC converter
